- `Type u_1` and `Type u_4` are universe levels, which do not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
On a discrete space $X$, the cocompact filter is the cofinite filter: a subset of $X$ contains the complement of a compact set exactly when its own complement is finite.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [DiscreteTopology X]`: $X$ is a topological space whose topology is discrete: every subset of $X$ is open.
- The conclusion: `cocompact X = cofinite`. The left side is the filter of the subsets of $X$ that contain $X \setminus K$ for some compact $K \subseteq X$; the right side is the filter of the subsets of $X$ with finite complement.

The reason is the standard one: in a discrete space the singletons form an open cover of any subset, so the compact subsets are exactly the finite ones, and the two filters have the same generating sets. The statement holds for every discrete space, of any cardinality.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `[TopologicalSpace X]` and `[DiscreteTopology X]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. `DiscreteTopology X` says that the topology is the discrete one; it adds no data.
- Mathlib's filters may contain the empty set. When $X$ is finite, $X$ is compact and $\emptyset$ has finite complement, so both sides are the degenerate filter of all subsets of $X$, and the equality still holds; it holds too for empty $X$.
- `cofinite` takes the type $X$ as an implicit argument, which Lean reads off the left side.
- Compactness is the finite-subcover property, with no Hausdorff condition, which makes no difference for discrete spaces.

## What it says
For a type $\alpha$, `cofinite` is the cofinite filter on $\alpha$: the family of the subsets $s \subseteq \alpha$ whose complement $\alpha \setminus s$ is finite.

- The type $\alpha$ is an implicit argument, which Lean reads off the context; the result has type `Filter α`, a filter on $\alpha$.
- The value: `comk Set.Finite …` builds the filter whose members are the sets with a finite complement. The three proofs passed to it say that the empty set is finite, that a subset of a finite set is finite, and that a union of two finite sets is finite; these are what make the family contain $\alpha$ itself and be closed under supersets and finite intersections.

This is the standard cofinite filter, also called the Fréchet filter. Along it, "eventually" means "for all but finitely many points": on $\mathbb{N}$ it is the filter of the sets that contain all large enough $n$, so limits along it are limits of sequences.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- A filter in Mathlib may contain the empty set; one that does not is called `NeBot`. The cofinite filter is proper exactly when $\alpha$ is infinite. When $\alpha$ is finite, the empty set has finite complement, so the filter contains every subset: it is the degenerate filter, the bottom element of Mathlib's order on filters, where every property holds eventually. Classically the Fréchet filter is usually considered only on infinite sets; the definition is the same, read literally, on finite ones.
- `Type u_2` is a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A property holds eventually along the cofinite filter exactly when it fails at only finitely many points.

- The type $\alpha$ and the property $p$ of its elements are implicit arguments, which Lean reads off the statement being rewritten.
- The conclusion: `(∀ᶠ (x : α) in cofinite, p x)`, "$p(x)$ holds eventually along the cofinite filter", that is, the set $\{x \mid p(x)\}$ belongs to the filter of subsets of $\alpha$ with finite complement, holds if and only if `{x : α | ¬p x}.Finite`: the set of the $x$ at which $p$ fails is finite.

This is the defining property of the cofinite filter read for the set $\{x \mid p(x)\}$, whose complement is $\{x \mid \neg p(x)\}$: "eventually along the cofinite filter" means "for all but finitely many $x$". It holds on every type, with no order or countability on $\alpha$.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `∀ᶠ x in l, p x` is Mathlib's notation for "$p$ holds eventually along the filter $l$", that is, $\{x \mid p(x)\} \in l$.
- `Set.Finite` is finiteness of a set in the usual sense, the empty set included.
- When $\alpha$ is finite, both sides hold for every $p$; the cofinite filter is then the degenerate filter of all subsets, along which every property holds eventually.
- The attribute `simp` lets Lean's simplifier rewrite the left side into the right side by itself.
- `Type u_2` is a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
Every point is avoided eventually along the cofinite filter: all but finitely many elements of a type differ from a given one.

- `(x : α)`: a point $x$ of a type $\alpha$, which is an implicit argument.
- The conclusion: `∀ᶠ (a : α) in cofinite, a ≠ x`, that is, the set $\{a \in \alpha \mid a \neq x\}$ belongs to the cofinite filter on $\alpha$: its complement, the singleton $\{x\}$, is finite.

This is the basic fact that the cofinite filter, the Fréchet filter, contains the complement of every point; along it, $a \neq x$ holds for all $a$ but one. It does not say that every $a$ differs from $x$, nor that $\alpha$ is infinite, and it holds on every type.

## What it says
`Finite α` is the proposition that the type α is finite: it is in bijection with $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ for some natural number $n$.

- `(α : Sort u_3)`: a type α, of any universe, propositions included (a proposition is read as the type of its proofs).
- The result is a `Prop`: being finite is a property of α, not a structure on it.
- Its one constructor, `intro`, takes a natural number $n$, which is implicit, and an equivalence `α ≃ Fin n`, a bijection between α and `Fin n`, the type of the natural numbers below $n$; it gives `Finite α`. So `Finite α` holds exactly when such an $n$ and such a bijection exist.

This is the usual definition of a finite set, as one in bijection with an initial segment $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ of $\mathbb{N}$. As the docstring explains, it is the propositional counterpart of `Fintype`, which carries an explicit list of the elements as data; every `Fintype` gives a `Finite`, and conversely `Fintype.ofFinite` makes a `Fintype` from it without an algorithm.

## What it says
`FiniteDimensional K V` is the proposition that the vector space $V$ over $K$ is finite-dimensional, that is, spanned by finitely many vectors.

- `[DivisionRing K]`: $K$ is a division ring, a ring with $1$, not necessarily commutative, in which every nonzero element has an inverse; every field is one.
- `[AddCommGroup V]`: $V$ is an abelian group under addition.
- `[Module K V]`: a scalar multiplication of $K$ on $V$, on the left, making $V$ a vector space over $K$ (a left vector space when $K$ is not commutative).
- The result is a `Prop`, a property of $V$, and its value is `Module.Finite K V`: $V$ is finitely generated as a module over $K$, that is, some finite set of vectors spans $V$.

This is the usual definition of a finite-dimensional vector space, by a finite spanning family, which is equivalent to having a finite basis. It is stated for scalars in any division ring, where the literature usually takes a field.

## What it says
`Finset α` is the type of the finite subsets of a type α, each given as a finite collection of its elements, without order and without repetition.

- `(α : Type u_3)`: the type α whose finite subsets are meant; it may be infinite.
- The result, `Type u_3`, is a type in the same universe as α.
- The fields of a finite set $s$ are `val : Multiset α`, a multiset of elements of α, that is, a finite list taken up to reordering; and `nodup : Nodup val`, the proof that no element occurs twice in `val`.

A finite subset of α corresponds to exactly one multiset without repeated elements, the one listing each of its members once; so `Finset α` is in bijection with the finite subsets of α, the classical notion. The order of a list is forgotten by passing to multisets, and multiplicities by asking for no duplicates, so membership is all that a finite set records.

## What it says
`s.card` is the number of elements of a finite set $s$, its cardinality $|s|$.

This is the cardinality of a finite set in the usual sense. It does not depend on an order of the elements, since a multiset has none.

## What it says
In a normed commutative ring whose identity has norm $1$, the norm of a finite product is at most the product of the norms: $\bigl\|\prod_{i \in s} f(i)\bigr\| \le \prod_{i \in s} \|f(i)\|$.

- `[NormedCommRing α]`: $\alpha$ is a commutative ring with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ that vanishes only at $0$, satisfies the triangle inequality and is submultiplicative, $\|xy\| \le \|x\|\,\|y\|$; its topology is that of the distance $\|x - y\|$.
- `[NormOneClass α]`: the identity has norm one, $\|1\| = 1$.
- `(s : Finset ι)`: a finite set $s$ of indices, in a type $\iota$.
- `(f : ι → α)`: a family $f$ of elements of $\alpha$, indexed by $\iota$.
- The conclusion: the norm of the product $\prod_{i \in s} f(i)$, taken in $\alpha$, is at most the product of the real numbers $\|f(i)\|$ over $i \in s$.

This is submultiplicativity of the norm extended from two factors to finitely many, by induction on the size of $s$. The hypothesis $\|1\| = 1$ is what the empty product needs, where the inequality reads $\|1\| \le 1$.

## What it says
`Finset.sum s f`, written `∑ x ∈ s, f x`, is the finite sum $\sum_{x \in s} f(x)$ of the values of $f$ over the elements of a finite set $s$.

- `[AddCommMonoid M]`: $M$ is a commutative monoid under addition: its addition is associative and commutative and has a zero.
- `(s : Finset ι)`: a finite set $s$ of indices, in a type $\iota$.
- `(f : ι → M)`: a function $f$ from the indices to $M$.
- The result is an element of $M$. Its value, `(s.1.map f)` summed, is obtained by applying $f$ to every element of the underlying multiset `s.1` of $s$, which gives the multiset of the values $f(x)$ for $x \in s$, and adding up that multiset.

This is the usual finite sum. Each index of $s$ contributes once, so a value taken at several indices is counted once for each; and the sum does not depend on an order of $s$, which a multiset does not have, since the addition is associative and commutative.

## What it says
Evaluation at a point commutes with finite sums of functions: $\bigl(\sum_{c \in s} g_c\bigr)(a) = \sum_{c \in s} g_c(a)$, for functions whose values at different points may lie in different groups.

- `[(a : α) → AddCommMonoid (M a)]`: $M$ is a family of types $M(a)$ indexed by the points $a$ of a type $\alpha$, and each $M(a)$ is a commutative monoid under addition.
- `(a : α)`: the point $a$ at which the functions are evaluated.
- `(s : Finset ι)`: a finite set $s$ of indices, in a type $\iota$.
- `(g : ι → (a : α) → M a)`: for each index $c$, a function $g_c$ on $\alpha$ with $g_c(a) \in M(a)$ for every $a$, that is, an element of the product $\prod_{a \in \alpha} M(a)$.
- The conclusion: the sum $\sum_{c \in s} g_c$, taken in that product, evaluated at $a$, equals the sum in $M(a)$ of the values $g_c(a)$ for $c \in s$.

Functions are added pointwise, so this is the familiar fact that the value of a finite sum of functions is the sum of their values, here for a product of possibly different monoids. Only addition and zero are used: no topology or summability enters.

## What it says
Two finite sums are equal when they run over the same finite set and their summands agree on that set: if $s_1 = s_2$ and $f(x) = g(x)$ for every $x \in s_2$, then $\sum_{x \in s_1} f(x) = \sum_{x \in s_2} g(x)$.

- The finite sets $s_1, s_2$ of indices, in a type $\iota$, and the functions $f, g : \iota \to M$ are implicit arguments, which Lean reads off the sums.
- `[AddCommMonoid M]`: $M$ is a commutative monoid under addition, where finite sums make sense.
- `(h : s₁ = s₂)`: the two index sets are equal.
- The second hypothesis, `∀ x ∈ s₂, f x = g x`: $f$ and $g$ take the same value at every point of $s_2$; nothing is asked of them outside $s_2$.
- The conclusion: `s₁.sum f = s₂.sum g`, that is, $\sum_{x \in s_1} f(x) = \sum_{x \in s_2} g(x)$.

This is the expected congruence law for finite sums, true because a sum over $s$ depends only on the values of the summand at the points of $s$.

## What it says
Summing, over a finite set $s$ of indices, the functions that carry $f(a')$ at the index $a'$ and $0$ elsewhere, and evaluating at $a$, gives $f(a)$ when $a \in s$ and $0$ otherwise.

- `[DecidableEq ι]`: equality of indices in the type $\iota$ can be decided, which the function `Pi.single` and the case distinction `if a ∈ s` use.
- `[(a : ι) → AddCommMonoid (M a)]`: $M$ is a family of types $M(i)$ indexed by $i \in \iota$, each a commutative monoid under addition.
- `(a : ι)`: the index $a$ at which everything is evaluated.
- `(f : (a : ι) → M a)`: a choice of an element $f(i) \in M(i)$ for every index $i$, that is, an element of the product $\prod_{i} M(i)$.
- `(s : Finset ι)`: a finite set $s$ of indices.
- The conclusion: $\sum_{a' \in s} \delta_{a'}(f(a'))(a)$ equals $f(a)$ if $a \in s$ and $0$ otherwise, where $\delta_{a'}(x)$, written `Pi.single a' x`, is the element of the product with $x$ at $a'$ and $0$ at every other index. The sum is taken in $M(a)$.

At the coordinate $a$, the only term that can be nonzero is the one with $a' = a$, and it is present exactly when $a \in s$: this is the usual computation with the "standard basis vectors" $\delta_{a'}$ of a product, for possibly different monoids at different indices.

A `Fintype` structure on a type α is an explicit witness that α is finite: a finite set of elements of α that contains them all.

## What it says
A topological space is first countable when every point has a countable neighborhood basis. `FirstCountableTopology α` is this property of a type `α` carrying a topology.

- `[t : TopologicalSpace α]`: a topology on the type `α`, which may live in any universe `u`; `t` names it.
- The conclusion, `Prop`: the class is a property of the space, not extra structure on it.

Its one field, `nhds_generated_countable`, asks that for every point $a$ of `α` the neighborhood filter `𝓝 a` be countably generated (`IsCountablyGenerated`): there is a countable family of sets such that the neighborhoods of $a$ are exactly the sets containing a finite intersection of members of the family. The finite intersections of a countable family again form a countable family, so this says that $a$ has a countable neighborhood basis: countably many neighborhoods of $a$ such that every neighborhood of $a$ contains one of them.

This is the standard notion of a first-countable space, as the docstring says. The basis may depend on the point, and asking for open neighborhoods gives the same notion, since the interiors of the members of a basis again form one.

## What it says
A `FloorRing α` is integer floor and ceiling functions on a ring `α` with a linear order: for each $a$ in `α`, $\lfloor a \rfloor$ is the greatest integer $z$ with $z \le a$, and $\lceil a \rceil$ the least integer $z$ with $a \le z$.

- `[Ring α]`: a ring structure on the type `α`, with a $1$, not necessarily commutative.
- `[LinearOrder α]`: a total order $\le$ on `α`.
- The conclusion, `Type u_3`: a `FloorRing α` is data on `α`, in the universe of `α`, not a mere property.

Its fields are two functions `floor : α → ℤ` and `ceil : α → ℤ`, and two laws, each a Galois connection (`GaloisConnection`), a pair of maps $f, g$ with $f(x) \le y \iff x \le g(y)$. The law `gc_coe_floor` says that for every integer $z$ and every $a$ in `α`, $(z : α) \le a$ if and only if $z \le \lfloor a \rfloor$: so $\lfloor a \rfloor$ is the greatest integer below $a$. The law `gc_ceil_coe` says that $\lceil a \rceil \le z$ if and only if $a \le (z : α)$: so $\lceil a \rceil$ is the least integer above $a$.

These are the standard floor and ceiling, as on the rationals and the reals: rounding down and rounding up to an integer, negative elements included. The docstring states the floor's law in the same form.

- The class itself asks for no compatibility between the order and the ring operations: the "linear ordered ring" of the docstring is the setting it is meant for, not part of its definition.
- `floor` and `ceil` are both stored as data, but each is determined by its law, since an adjoint is unique: a type carries at most one such structure, so nothing is chosen arbitrarily.
- The floor rounds down, not toward zero: in $\mathbb{Q}$, $\lfloor -1/2 \rfloor = -1$, since $(z : \mathbb{Q}) \le -1/2$ exactly when $z \le -1$.
- The values lie in `ℤ`, not in `α`; to compare $\lfloor a \rfloor$ with $a$ one maps it back by the coercion `(↑)`, the ring map $\mathbb{Z} \to α$.
- The comment above `gc_coe_floor` names `FloorRing.ceil`; the field itself, `GaloisConnection (↑) floor`, is the law of `floor`.
- Since $\lfloor 0 \rfloor$ must be at least every integer $z$ with $(z : α) \le 0$, the zero ring and rings of positive characteristic, where $(z : α) = 0$ for infinitely many $z > 0$, carry no such structure.

## What it says
A ring with integer floor and ceiling functions also has natural-number ones: this instance makes every floor ring a floor semiring.

- `[Ring α]`: a ring structure on a type `α`, with a $1$.
- `[LinearOrder α]`: a total order $\le$ on `α`.
- `[FloorRing α]`: integer floor and ceiling on `α`: $\lfloor a \rfloor$, the greatest integer below $a$, and $\lceil a \rceil$, the least integer above it.
- The conclusion, `FloorSemiring α`: natural-number floor and ceiling functions $\alpha \to \mathbb{N}$, written $\lfloor a \rfloor_+$ and $\lceil a \rceil_+$ here.

Its value sets $\lfloor a \rfloor_+$ to `⌊a⌋.toNat` and $\lceil a \rceil_+$ to `⌈a⌉.toNat`, where `Int.toNat` sends a negative integer to $0$ and a nonnegative one to the same natural number. The laws of a floor semiring then hold: $\lfloor a \rfloor_+ = 0$ for $a < 0$; for $a \ge 0$ and every natural $n$, $n \le \lfloor a \rfloor_+$ if and only if $n \le a$; and for every $a$ and $n$, $\lceil a \rceil_+ \le n$ if and only if $a \le n$.

So for $a \ge 0$, $\lfloor a \rfloor_+$ is the integer floor, the greatest natural number below $a$, and for every $a$, $\lceil a \rceil_+$ is the least natural number above $a$: the standard rounding, restricted to natural values. For example at $a = -3/2$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, $\lfloor a \rfloor = -2$ and $\lceil a \rceil = -1$, while $\lfloor a \rfloor_+ = \lceil a \rceil_+ = 0$.

## What it says
A `FloorSemiring α` is natural-number floor and ceiling functions on a semiring `α` with a partial order: for $a \ge 0$, $\lfloor a \rfloor$ is the greatest natural number $n$ with $n \le a$, and for every $a$, $\lceil a \rceil$ is the least natural number $n$ with $a \le n$.

- `[Semiring α]`: a semiring structure on the type `α`: addition and multiplication with $0$ and $1$, but no subtraction needed, as in $\mathbb{N}$ or the nonnegative reals.
- `[PartialOrder α]`: a partial order $\le$ on `α`, not necessarily total.
- The conclusion, `Type u_3`: a `FloorSemiring α` is data on `α`, in the universe of `α`, not a mere property.

Its fields are two functions `floor : α → ℕ` and `ceil : α → ℕ` and three laws:
`floor_of_neg`, that $\lfloor a \rfloor = 0$ when $a < 0$;
`gc_floor`, that for $0 \le a$ and every natural $n$, $n \le \lfloor a \rfloor$ if and only if $(n : α) \le a$;
and `gc_ceil`, a Galois connection (`GaloisConnection`) between `ceil` and the map $n \mapsto (n : α)$: for every $a$ and $n$, $\lceil a \rceil \le n$ if and only if $a \le (n : α)$.

These are the standard floor and ceiling, rounding down and up, with natural values. The docstring states the floor's law without the hypothesis $0 \le x$; the field `gc_floor` carries it, and needs it: for $x < 0$ and $n = 0$, $0 \le \lfloor x \rfloor$ holds while $0 \le x$ does not.

## What it says
A semiring with natural-number floor and ceiling functions has characteristic zero: distinct natural numbers stay distinct in it.

- `[Semiring α]`: a semiring structure on a type `α`: addition and multiplication with $0$ and $1$.
- `[PartialOrder α]`: a partial order $\le$ on `α`.
- `[FloorSemiring α]`: natural floor and ceiling functions on `α`, with $\lfloor a \rfloor = 0$ for $a < 0$, $n \le \lfloor a \rfloor \iff (n : α) \le a$ for $a \ge 0$, and $\lceil a \rceil \le n \iff a \le (n : α)$ for all $a$.
- The conclusion, `CharZero α`: the map $\mathbb{N} \to α$, $n \mapsto n \cdot 1$, is injective.

The laws force this. The ceiling law at $a = 0$ gives $\lceil 0 \rceil = 0$, hence $0 \le (k : α)$ for every natural $k$, so the floor law applies at every $(m : α)$. If $(m : α) = (n : α)$ with $m < n$, the map $k \mapsto (k : α)$ repeats with period $n - m$ from $m$ on, so infinitely many $k$ have $(k : α) \le (m : α)$; the floor law allows only those $k \le \lfloor (m : α) \rfloor$.

This is the familiar fact that a structure with floors, such as the rationals or the reals, contains a copy of $\mathbb{N}$, here for semirings and partial orders, with no compatibility between the order and the operations assumed.

## What it says
In a semiring with natural-number floor and ceiling functions, $0 \le 1$ for the given order.

- `[Semiring α]`: a semiring structure on a type `α`: addition and multiplication with $0$ and $1$.

The ceiling law forces it. Put otherwise, the map $n \mapsto (n : α)$ is monotone, as the upper half of a Galois connection always is, and carries $0 \le 1$ in $\mathbb{N}$ to `α`.

In an ordered semiring $0 \le 1$ is part of the setting; here it is derived from the floor structure for an arbitrary partial order, which on its own need not make $0 \le 1$.

## What it says
`FunLike F α β` is the structure that lets the elements of a type `F` be used as functions from `α` to `β`, an element being determined by its values. It is how Mathlib treats homomorphisms of every kind as functions.

- `(F : Sort u_1)`: the type of the objects to be read as functions, such as the ring homomorphisms between two rings.
- `(α : Sort u_2)`: the domain of those functions.
- `(β : Sort u_3)`: their codomain.
- The conclusion, `Sort (max (max (max 1 u_1) u_2) u_3)`: `FunLike F α β` is a type of data, large enough to hold a map from `F` to the functions from `α` to `β`; the universe levels do not affect the mathematics.

Its value is `DFunLike F α fun _ => β`: the dependent version, in which the codomain may vary with the point of `α`, taken with the same codomain `β` at every point. As the docstring says, a structure of this kind is a coercion from `F` to the functions $α \to β$ that is injective: two elements of `F` with the same values at every point are equal.

This is the usual way of regarding a homomorphism as its underlying function, with the fact, implicit in the mathematics, that a homomorphism is determined by its values. The injectivity concerns the map from `F` to functions; each single function may be constant or fail to be injective.

If a connected space maps continuously onto a space, that space is connected too.

This is the standard fact that the continuous image of a connected space is connected: since $f$ is onto, its image is all of `β`, and a point of `α` gives a point of `β`.

## What it says
For a space $Y$ that is compact and locally compact, and any index set $ι$, the power $Y^ι$, the product of copies of $Y$ indexed by $ι$, is locally compact.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y]`: a topology on a type `Y`.
- `[LocallyCompactSpace Y]`: `Y` is locally compact: every neighborhood of a point contains a compact neighborhood of it.
- `[CompactSpace Y]`: `Y` is compact.
- The conclusion, `LocallyCompactSpace (ι → Y)`: the space of all functions from a type `ι` to `Y`, with the product topology, is locally compact.

A neighborhood of a point $x$ of $Y^ι$ contains a basic open set that restricts finitely many coordinates $x_i$ to neighborhoods $U_i$. Choosing a compact neighborhood $K_i \subseteq U_i$ of $x_i$ for each of them, and all of $Y$ in the other coordinates, gives a neighborhood of $x$ inside it that is compact by Tychonoff's theorem.

This is the standard theorem that a product of locally compact spaces is locally compact when all but finitely many factors are compact, in the case of equal factors, all compact. For infinite $ι$ and nonempty $Y$, compactness of $Y$ cannot be dropped.

## What it says
`FundamentalGroup X x` is the fundamental group $\pi_1(X, x)$ of a space `X` at a point `x`: the homotopy classes of loops at `x`, under composition.

Its value is `End (FundamentalGroupoid.mk x)`: the endomorphisms of `x`, taken as an object of the fundamental groupoid of `X`. In that groupoid the objects are the points of `X`, and a morphism from $y$ to $z$ is a homotopy class, relative to the endpoints, of paths from $y$ to $z$; so an endomorphism of `x` is a homotopy class of loops at `x`. Every morphism of a groupoid is invertible, so these endomorphisms form a group under composition, the vertex group of the docstring.

This is the standard fundamental group, presented through the fundamental groupoid as the group of automorphisms of the basepoint.

A path $p$ from $x_0$ to $x_1$ gives an isomorphism of fundamental groups $\pi_1(X, x_0) \cong \pi_1(X, x_1)$: the change-of-basepoint isomorphism.

- The conclusion, `FundamentalGroup X x₀ ≃* FundamentalGroup X x₁`: an isomorphism of groups from the fundamental group at `x₀` to the one at `x₁`.

Its value is conjugation (`conj`) by `⟦p⟧`, the homotopy class of `p`, read as an isomorphism from `x₀` to `x₁` in the fundamental groupoid (`Groupoid.isoEquivHom`, since in a groupoid every morphism is one). This is the standard isomorphism showing that the fundamental group does not depend on the basepoint within a path component. It depends only on the homotopy class of $p$, and other path classes may give other isomorphisms.

## What it says
A continuous map $f \colon X \to Y$ induces a functor from the fundamental groupoid of $X$ to that of $Y$: a point $x$ goes to $f(x)$, and the class of a path $\gamma$ to the class of $f \circ \gamma$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on the types $X$ and $Y$, which are implicit arguments.
- `(f : C(X, Y))`: a continuous map $f$ from $X$ to $Y$; `C(X, Y)` is the type of continuous maps, each a function together with the fact that it is continuous.
- The result has type `CategoryTheory.Functor (FundamentalGroupoid X) (FundamentalGroupoid Y)`: a functor between the two fundamental groupoids.

Its value:

- `obj x := ⟨f x.as⟩`: an object $x$, which wraps the point `x.as` of $X$, goes to the object wrapping $f$ of that point.
- `map p := p.map f`: a morphism $p$, the homotopy class with endpoints fixed of a path $\gamma$, goes to the class of the image path $f \circ \gamma$.
- `map_id` and `map_comp`: the proofs that identities go to identities, which holds by definition (`rfl`), since the image of a constant path is constant, and that composites go to composites, since $f$ carries a concatenation of paths to the concatenation of their images.

This is the functor $\Pi(f)$ that a map induces on fundamental groupoids in the literature. On the morphisms from a point to itself it restricts to the homomorphism $[\gamma] \mapsto [f \circ \gamma]$ of fundamental groups induced by $f$.

For a topological space $X$ with base point $x$ and index types $M$, $N$, the $M$-fold loop space of the $N$-fold loop space of $X$ is homeomorphic to the $(M \sqcup N)$-fold loop space of $X$: $\Omega^M(\Omega^N X) \cong \Omega^{M \sqcup N} X$.

Here `GenLoop N X x`, written $\Omega^N X$, is the set of continuous maps from the cube $I^N$ (the functions $N \to [0,1]$, with the product topology) to $X$ that send the boundary of the cube, the points with some coordinate $0$ or $1$, to $x$.

- `(x : X)`: the base point $x$ of $X$.
- The conclusion: `≃ₜ` is a homeomorphism, from the generalized loops $I^M \to \Omega^N X$ based at `const`, the constant loop at $x$, to the generalized loops $I^{M \sqcup N} \to X$ based at $x$. The index types $M$ and $N$ are arbitrary, not necessarily finite.

Its value uncurries: a loop $p$ goes to the map $y \mapsto p(y|_M)(y|_N)$, where $y|_M$ and $y|_N$ are the restrictions of $y : M \sqcup N \to [0,1]$ to the two summands; the inverse curries a loop $q$ in the same coordinates. A point $y$ is on the boundary of $I^{M \sqcup N}$ exactly when $y|_M$ or $y|_N$ is on the boundary of its cube, so both maps respect the boundary conditions.

This is the standard identification $\Omega^m \Omega^n X \cong \Omega^{m+n} X$ of iterated loop spaces, with arbitrary index sets in place of $\{1,\dots,m\}$ and $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and the coordinates of $M$ first.

`Group G` is the structure of a group on a type `G`: a monoid in which every element $a$ has an inverse $a^{-1}$ with $a^{-1} a = 1$.

Only the left inverse law is asked for, but in a monoid it implies the right one: $a a^{-1} = (a^{-1})^{-1} a^{-1} a a^{-1} = (a^{-1})^{-1} a^{-1} = 1$. Division and integer powers are extra operations that the laws above pin down to their usual meanings, so they add nothing to the notion.

`HasSum f a L` says that the family $(f(b))_{b \in \beta}$ sums to $a$ along the summation filter $L$: the finite partial sums $\sum_{b \in s} f(b)$ converge to $a$ as the finite set $s \subseteq \beta$ grows in the way $L$ prescribes. Its value is `Tendsto (fun s : Finset β ↦ ∑ b ∈ s, f b) L.filter (𝓝 a)`: the map sending a finite set $s$ to $\sum_{b \in s} f(b)$ tends to $a$ along the filter that $L$ carries on finite sets.

With the default filter this is the standard unconditional summation of a family in a topological monoid, the limit of the net of finite partial sums; it does not depend on any ordering of the indices.

- `(h : X ≃ₜ Y)`: a homeomorphism `h` from `X` to `Y`.
- `(h_iff : ∀ (x : X), p x ↔ q (h x))`: for every point $x$ of `X`, the condition `p` holds at $x$ exactly when the condition `q` holds at $h(x)$; here `p` and `q` are arbitrary conditions on the points of `X` and of `Y`. Equivalently $p = q \circ h$, as the docstring puts it.

Its value, `h.subtypeEquiv h_iff`, is the bijection that sends $x$ to $h(x)$, which satisfies `q` by `h_iff`, with inverse sending $y$ to $h^{-1}(y)$. Both maps are continuous: each is the restriction of a continuous map to a subspace, taken as a map into a subspace.

This is the standard fact that a homeomorphism restricts to a homeomorphism from any subspace onto its image; `h_iff` says that the image of the first set is the second.

## What it says
In an extension of rings whose top ring $S$ is a Dedekind domain, the ramification index of an ideal $q$ of $S$ over the ideal $p$ it lies over is the exponent of $q$ in the factorization of $pS$ into prime ideals.

- `[CommRing R] [CommRing S]`: `R` and `S` are commutative rings, with a $1$.
- `[Algebra R S]`: `S` is an algebra over `R`, through a ring homomorphism `algebraMap R S` from `R` to `S`.
- `(p : Ideal R)`: an ideal `p` of `R`.
- `(q : Ideal S)`: an ideal `q` of `S`.
- `[IsDedekindDomain S]`: `S` is a Dedekind domain, so its nonzero ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals.
- `[q.LiesOver p]`: `q` lies over `p`: the preimage of `q` in `R` is `p`.
- `(hp0 : map (algebraMap R S) p ≠ ⊥)`: the ideal $pS$ of `S` generated by the image of `p` is not the zero ideal.
- The conclusion: `q.ramificationIdx R`, the ramification index of `q` over `R`, equals the number of times `q` occurs in `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.normalizedFactors (map (algebraMap R S) p)`, the multiset of the prime ideals in the factorization of $pS$, each repeated as often as its exponent. So if $pS = \prod_Q Q^{e_Q}$, the ramification index of `q` is $e_q$.

This is the classical description of ramification indices in an extension of Dedekind domains: $pS = \prod_i Q_i^{e_i}$, with $e_i$ the ramification index of $Q_i$ over $p$. Here `R` may be any commutative ring, and the only condition on `p` is that $pS \ne 0$.

- `(R : Type u_2)`: the base ring `R`, given explicitly, since `q` does not determine it.
- `[CommRing R]`: `R` is a commutative ring, with a $1$.
- `[Algebra R S]`: `S` is an algebra over `R`, through a ring homomorphism from `R` to `S`.

`IsArithFrobAt R σ Q` says that σ is an arithmetic Frobenius at the ideal Q: $\sigma \cdot x \equiv x^q \pmod{Q}$ for every $x \in S$, where $q$ is the number of elements of $R/(Q \cap R)$.

- `(σ : M)`: an element σ of the monoid.

Its value is `AlgHom.IsArithFrobAt` applied to the R-algebra map $x \mapsto \sigma \cdot x$ and Q: the congruence above, with $Q \cap R$ the ideal of elements of R sent into Q.

This is the defining congruence of the classical Frobenius at a prime: for $R = \mathbb{Z}$ and Q above $p$, $q = p$. It is the arithmetic Frobenius, raising to the power $q$, not its inverse, the geometric Frobenius. It is only the condition: existence and uniqueness, under Galois and unramified hypotheses, are separate results.

`IsCancelMulZero M₀` says that in M₀ a nonzero factor can be cancelled from either side of an equation.

In a topological space, a set that is both open and closed and contains a point $x$ contains the whole connected component of $x$.

If $C$ is the component of $x$, then $C \cap s$ and $C \setminus s$ are disjoint, open and closed in $C$, and cover $C$; since $C$ is connected and $x \in C \cap s$, the second is empty. Put otherwise, the component of $x$ lies in the intersection of the clopen sets containing $x$.

## What it says
In a preconnected topological space, a nonempty subset that is both open and closed is the whole space.

This is one direction of the standard clopen criterion: a space is connected exactly when its only clopen subsets are $\emptyset$ and the whole space. Here $s$ and its complement are disjoint open sets that cover α, and $s$ is nonempty, so the complement is empty. The hypothesis that $s$ is nonempty rules out $s = \emptyset$, the other clopen subset every space has.

## What it says
The image of a closed map is a closed subset of its target.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on the types X and Y, between which runs a map $f : X \to Y$.
- `(hf : IsClosedMap f)`: $f$ is a closed map: the image under $f$ of every closed subset of X is closed in Y.
- The conclusion, `IsClosed (Set.range f)`: the range $f(X) = \{f(x) : x \in X\}$ is closed in Y.

This is immediate from the definition: X is closed in itself, so its image $f(X)$ is closed. No continuity, compactness or separation hypothesis is involved.

## What it says
A closed map $f : E \to X$ from a Hausdorff space, with finite fibres over a set $s \subseteq X$ and a local homeomorphism at every point over $s$, is a covering map over $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: topologies on the types E and X, between which runs a map $f : E \to X$; the set $s \subseteq X$ is implicit.
- `[T2Space E]`: E is Hausdorff.
- `(hf : IsClosedMap f)`: $f$ is a closed map: the image of every closed subset of E is closed in X.
- `(hs : ∀ x ∈ s, (f ⁻¹' {x}).Finite)`: every point $x \in s$ has finitely many preimages, possibly none.
- `(h : IsLocalHomeomorphOn f (f ⁻¹' s))`: every point $e$ with $f(e) \in s$ has an open neighbourhood that $f$ maps homeomorphically onto an open subset of X.
- The conclusion, `IsCoveringMapOn f s`: every $x \in s$ is evenly covered: it has an open neighbourhood $U$ in X whose preimage is a disjoint union of open sets, one for each point of the fibre over $x$, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$.

This is the classical criterion that a closed local homeomorphism with finite fibres from a Hausdorff space is a covering map, localized to $s$. The proof separates the finitely many points over $x$ by disjoint open sets, using that E is Hausdorff, and uses closedness to remove the image of everything outside them.

## What it says
A continuous surjective closed map is a quotient map.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on the types X and Y, between which runs a map $f : X \to Y$.
- `(hcl : IsClosedMap f)`: $f$ is a closed map: the image of every closed subset of X is closed in Y.
- `(hcont : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous.
- `(hsurj : Function.Surjective f)`: every point of Y is $f(x)$ for some $x \in X$.
- The conclusion, `Topology.IsQuotientMap f`: $f$ is a quotient map: it is surjective, and a set $V \subseteq Y$ is open exactly when its preimage $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in X.

This is the standard criterion, in its form for closed sets. If $f^{-1}(C)$ is closed, then $C = f(f^{-1}(C))$ by surjectivity, which is closed since $f$ is a closed map; continuity gives the converse. Closed sets determine the topology as open sets do, so the topology of Y is the quotient topology.

## What it says
Every cover of a compact set by open sets has a finite subcover.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type X, whose subsets $s$ the statement is about.
- `(hs : IsCompact s)`: the set $s \subseteq X$ is compact.
- `(U : ι → Set X)`: a family $(U_i)_{i \in ι}$ of subsets of X, indexed by an arbitrary type ι.
- `(hUo : ∀ (i : ι), IsOpen (U i))`: each $U_i$ is open in X.
- `(hsU : s ⊆ ⋃ (i : ι), U i)`: the family covers $s$: $s \subseteq \bigcup_{i} U_i$.
- The conclusion: there is a finite set $t$ of indices with $s \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in t} U_i$.

This is the open-cover property that defines compactness in most texts; the finite subfamily is chosen from the given family, and the index set may be of any size.

## What it says
If a family of closed sets has an intersection that misses a compact set $s$, then some finite subfamily already has an intersection that misses $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type X, whose subsets $s$ the statement is about.
- `(hs : IsCompact s)`: the set $s \subseteq X$ is compact.
- `(t : ι → Set X)`: a family $(t_i)_{i \in ι}$ of subsets of X, indexed by an arbitrary type ι.
- `(htc : ∀ (i : ι), IsClosed (t i))`: each $t_i$ is closed in X.
- `(hst : Disjoint s (⋂ (i : ι), t i))`: $s \cap \bigcap_{i} t_i = \emptyset$.
- The conclusion: there is a finite set $u$ of indices with $s \cap \bigcap_{i \in u} t_i = \emptyset$.

This is the closed-set form of compactness, the finite intersection property relative to $s$: taking complements, the open sets $X \setminus t_i$ cover $s$, so finitely many of them do, which is the conclusion.

## What it says
In a topological space $X$, if $s$ is a compact set and each point $x$ of $s$ is given a neighbourhood $U(x)$, then finitely many of these neighbourhoods, taken at points of $s$, cover $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type $X$; $s$ ranges over the subsets of $X$.
- `(hs : IsCompact s)`: $s$ is compact: every cover of $s$ by open sets of $X$ has a finite subcover.
- `(U : X → Set X)`: a function that gives each point $x$ of $X$ a subset $U(x)$ of $X$.
- `(hU : ∀ x ∈ s, U x ∈ nhds x)`: for each $x \in s$, $U(x)$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, that is, it contains an open set containing $x$; it need not be open itself.
- The conclusion: there is a finite set $t$ of points of $X$ (`t : Finset X`), all of them in $s$, with $s \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in t} U(x)$.

This is the usual neighbourhood form of the finite-subcover property: the interiors of the $U(x)$, for $x \in s$, form an open cover of $s$, and a finite subcover gives the finite set of centres. The statement also records that the centres can be taken in $s$, as the classical argument gives.

## What it says
If $s$ is a compact subset of a topological space $X$ and $f$ is a proper filter on $X$ that contains $s$, then $f$ has a cluster point in $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type $X$; $s$ ranges over the subsets of $X$.
- `(hs : IsCompact s)`: $s$ is compact.
- `[f.NeBot]`: the filter $f$ on $X$ is proper: it does not contain the empty set (`NeBot` stands for "not bottom").
- `(hf : f ≤ Filter.principal s)`: $f$ is finer than the principal filter of $s$, the filter of all supersets of $s$; that is, $s \in f$.
- The conclusion: there is a point $x \in s$ that is a cluster point of $f$: every neighbourhood of $x$ meets every member of $f$.

This is the characterisation of compactness by filters, in the direction that is used most: a set is compact exactly when every proper filter containing it has a cluster point in it. It holds in any topological space.

## What it says
Cantor's intersection theorem: in a topological space $X$, a nonempty family $S$ of nonempty compact closed sets that is directed downwards has a nonempty intersection.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type $X$; $S$ ranges over the families of subsets of $X$ (`Set (Set X)`).
- `[hS : Nonempty ↑S]`: the family $S$ has at least one member.
- `(hSd : DirectedOn (fun (x1 x2 : Set X) => x1 ⊇ x2) S)`: $S$ is directed by reverse inclusion: for any members $U, V$ of $S$ there is a member $W$ of $S$ with $W \subseteq U$ and $W \subseteq V$.
- `(hSn : ∀ U ∈ S, U.Nonempty)`: every member of $S$ has a point.
- `(hSc : ∀ U ∈ S, IsCompact U)`: every member of $S$ is compact.
- `(hScl : ∀ U ∈ S, IsClosed U)`: every member of $S$ is closed.
- The conclusion: `⋂₀ S`, the intersection $\bigcap_{U \in S} U$ of all the members of $S$, has a point.

The classical statement, for a decreasing sequence $K_1 \supseteq K_2 \supseteq \cdots$ of nonempty compact sets, is the case where $S$ is the set of the $K_n$: a chain is directed. Directedness gives the finite intersection property, and a fixed member of $S$ supplies the compact set in which it is used.

## What it says
A subset $s$ of a topological space $\alpha$ is connected when it is nonempty and cannot be split into two nonempty pieces that are open in it.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: a topology on the type $\alpha$.
- `(s : Set α)`: the subset $s$ of $\alpha$ whose connectedness is defined.
- The result is a `Prop`: a property of $s$, true or false.

Its value is `s.Nonempty ∧ IsPreconnected s`: $s$ has a point, and $s$ is preconnected, that is, whenever $u$ and $v$ are open sets of $\alpha$ with $s \subseteq u \cup v$ and $s$ meets both $u$ and $v$, then $s$ meets $u \cap v$. Preconnectedness says that the subspace $s$ admits no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

This is connectedness of $s$ in the topology it inherits from $\alpha$, with the convention that a connected space is nonempty.

## What it says
A map $f : E \to X$ of topological spaces is a covering map when every point $x$ of $X$ is evenly covered: it has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that $f^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$ by $f$.

Its value is `∀ x, IsEvenlyCovered f x (f ⁻¹' {x})`: every $x \in X$ is evenly covered by $f$, with the sheets indexed by its own fibre $f^{-1}(x)$. That is, the fibre is discrete in the topology it inherits from $E$, and $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ homeomorphic to $U \times f^{-1}(x)$ by a homeomorphism that turns $f$ into the projection onto $U$.

This is the usual definition of a covering space: a product $U \times D$ with $D$ discrete is the disjoint union of the sheets $U \times \{d\}$, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$. Indexing the sheets by the fibre itself, rather than by some discrete set, makes no choice, since any such index set is in bijection with the fibre.

## What it says
Let $p : E \to X$ be a covering map and $A$ a preconnected space. Two continuous maps $f_0, f_1 : A \to E$ that agree at some point of a set $S \subseteq A$ are homotopic relative to $S$ if and only if $p \circ f_0$ and $p \circ f_1$ are homotopic relative to $S$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace A]`: $E$, $X$ and $A$ are topological spaces.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: the map $p : E \to X$ is a covering map: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood that $p$ covers evenly.
- `[PreconnectedSpace A]`: $A$ is preconnected: it is not the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets (the empty space counts as preconnected).
- `(he : ∃ a ∈ S, f₀ a = f₁ a)`: for the continuous maps $f_0, f_1 : A \to E$ and the set $S \subseteq A$, there is a point $a \in S$ with $f_0(a) = f_1(a)$.
- The conclusion: $f_0$ and $f_1$ are homotopic relative to $S$ if and only if $p \circ f_0$ and $p \circ f_1$ are. Here `{ toFun := p, continuous_toFun := ⋯ }` is $p$ packaged as a continuous map, and `.comp` composes it after $f_0$ or $f_1$.

The forward direction is composition with $p$. The converse is the relative form of homotopy lifting: a homotopy rel $S$ of $p \circ f_0$ lifts to a homotopy starting at $f_0$; the lift stays fixed on $S$, since lifts of constant paths are constant, and it ends at $f_1$ by the uniqueness of lifts from a connected space that agree at a point, which is where the preconnectedness of $A$ and the point $a$ come in.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$, two paths in $X$ that are homotopic with their endpoints fixed have lifts from the same point $e$ that end at the same point.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: the map $p : E \to X$ is a covering map: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood that $p$ covers evenly.
- `(h : γ₀.HomotopicRel γ₁ {0, 1})`: the paths $\gamma_0, \gamma_1 : [0,1] \to X$, continuous maps, are homotopic by a homotopy that fixes the times $0$ and $1$, that is, the endpoints.
- `(e : E)`: a point $e$ of $E$.
- `(h₀ : γ₀ 0 = p e)` and `(h₁ : γ₁ 0 = p e)`: $e$ lies over the common start of the two paths.
- The conclusion: the lift of $\gamma_0$ from $e$ (`cov.liftPath γ₀ e h₀`) and the lift of $\gamma_1$ from $e$ take the same value at time $1$.

This is the standard consequence of the homotopy lifting property for paths: the homotopy lifts to a homotopy from the first lift, which stays a homotopy with fixed endpoints, so the two lifts end at the same point. It is what makes the endpoint of a lift depend only on the homotopy class of the path.

For a covering map $p : E \to X$, the lift of a constant path at $x$ that starts at a point $e$ over $x$ is the constant path at $e$.

- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: the map $p : E \to X$ is a covering map: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood that $p$ covers evenly.

- The conclusion: `cov.liftPath`, applied to the constant path at $x$ (`ContinuousMap.const (↑unitInterval) x`) and the starting point $e$, gives the constant path at $e$.

The constant path at $e$ lifts the constant path at $x$ and starts at $e$, and lifts of a path with a given start are unique, so it is the lift. This holds however many points the fibre over $x$ has.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$ and a homotopy class $\gamma$ of paths from $x$ to $y$, the monodromy along $\gamma$ is the map from the fibre over $x$ to the fibre over $y$ that sends a point $e$ to the endpoint of the lift of $\gamma$ that starts at $e$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: the map $p : E \to X$ is a covering map: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood that $p$ covers evenly.
- `(γ : Path.Homotopic.Quotient x y)`: a class $\gamma$ of paths from $x$ to $y$ in $X$, up to homotopy fixing the endpoints.
- Its type, `↑(p ⁻¹' {x}) → ↑(p ⁻¹' {y})`: a function from the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ to the fibre $p^{-1}(y)$.
- Its value: for $e$ over $x$ and a path $\gamma_0$ from $x$ to $y$ in the class $\gamma$, take the lift `cov.liftPath` of $\gamma_0$ from $e$ and its value at time $1$, which lies over $y$. The result does not depend on $\gamma_0$, since homotopic paths have lifts from $e$ that end at the same point (`liftPath_apply_one_eq_of_homotopicRel`).

This is the standard transport of fibres along paths in the base of a covering, which, as the docstring says, depends only on the homotopy class of the path. For loops at $x$ it gives the action of the fundamental group on the fibre over $x$.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$, the monodromy functor sends each point of $X$ to its fibre and each homotopy class of paths to the transport of fibres along it: a functor from the fundamental groupoid of $X$ to sets.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: the map $p : E \to X$ is a covering map: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood that $p$ covers evenly.
- Its type, `CategoryTheory.Functor (FundamentalGroupoid X) (Type u_1)`: a functor from the fundamental groupoid of $X$, whose objects are the points of $X$ and whose morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are the homotopy classes of paths from $x$ to $y$, to the category of sets in the universe of $E$.
- Its value: an object $x$ goes to the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$; a class $f$ of paths from $x$ to $y$ goes to `cov.monodromy f`, the map $p^{-1}(x) \to p^{-1}(y)$ that sends $e$ to the endpoint of the lift of $f$ from $e$. Identities go to identities, as the lift of a constant path is constant (`monodromy_refl`), and composites to composites (`monodromy_trans_apply`).

This is the standard monodromy functor of a covering space, as in the definition the docstring cites, with no connectedness asked of $X$ or $E$.

- The objects of `FundamentalGroupoid X` wrap the points of $X$, and `x.as` is the point that $x$ wraps.
- Composition in Lean's categories is written in diagrammatic order: $f$ followed by $g$ goes to the transport along $f$ followed by the transport along $g$, so the functor is covariant.
- A fibre may be empty; the functor then sends that point to the empty set.
- The `@[simps]` attribute makes Lean generate lemmas giving the functor's value on objects and on morphisms.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$, the monodromy functor sends an arrow $f$ of the fundamental groupoid of $X$, a homotopy class of paths from a point $x$ to a point $y$, to the function given by monodromy along $f$: transport from the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ to the fibre $p^{-1}(y)$ by lifting paths.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the map $p : E \to X$ is an implicit argument.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point $x$ of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over $x$, which is discrete.
- `(f : X✝ ⟶ Y✝)`: an arrow of the fundamental groupoid `FundamentalGroupoid X` between two of its objects, which are points of $X$; an arrow from $x$ to $y$ is a class of paths from $x$ to $y$ up to homotopy fixing the endpoints.
- The conclusion: `cov.monodromyFunctor.map f`, the image of $f$ under the monodromy functor from the fundamental groupoid to the category of types (Lean's sets), equals `TypeCat.ofHom (cov.monodromy f)`, the function `cov.monodromy f` taken as an arrow of that category. That function sends a point $e$ over $x$ to the endpoint of the lift, starting at $e$, of a path in the class $f$.

This is the arrow part of the classical fibre-translation functor of a covering. It is covariant: an arrow from $x$ to $y$ carries the fibre over $x$ to the fibre over $y$, and lifting homotopies makes the result depend only on the class of the path.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$ and a point $x$ of $X$, the monodromy action of the fundamental group $\pi_1(X, x)$ on the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$, as a group homomorphism into the permutations of the fibre.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the map $p : E \to X$ is an implicit argument.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point $x$ of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over $x$, which is discrete.
- `(x : X)`: the base point.
- The value: a homomorphism `FundamentalGroup X x →* Equiv.Perm ↑(p ⁻¹' {x})` from the fundamental group of $X$ at $x$ to the group of permutations of the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$. It is `MulAction.toPermHom` applied to the action `cov.fundamentalGroupMulAction x` of the fundamental group on the fibre: a loop class $\gamma$ goes to the permutation $e \mapsto \gamma \cdot e$ of the fibre, which sends $e$ to the endpoint of the lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$.

This is the classical monodromy representation of $\pi_1(X, x)$ on the fibre. Its target is the group of all permutations of the fibre, not the group of deck transformations; a loop and its reverse give inverse permutations.

## Lean subtleties
- Mathlib's `FundamentalGroup X x` is the group of automorphisms of $x$ in the fundamental groupoid, and its product $\gamma \delta$ is the class of $\delta$ followed by $\gamma$, read right to left like composition of functions. With this product, transport along loops is a left action (a `MulAction`), and this map is a homomorphism. Books that compose loops left to right make the same transport a right action; each loop gives the same permutation either way.
- `Equiv.Perm` is the group of bijections of a type to itself under composition; `↑(p ⁻¹' {x})` is the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ taken as a type.
- `→*` marks a monoid homomorphism; between groups it also preserves inverses.
- The action is not found by Lean automatically, since it depends on the proof `cov`; `letI` supplies it to the definition.
- If the fibre is empty, its permutation group is trivial, and so is the homomorphism.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$ and a homotopy class $\gamma$ of paths from $x$ to $y$ in $X$, monodromy along $\gamma$ is a bijection from the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ onto the fibre $p^{-1}(y)$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the map $p : E \to X$ and the points $x$, $y$ of $X$ are implicit arguments.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point $x$ of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over $x$, which is discrete.
- `(γ : Path.Homotopic.Quotient x y)`: a class of paths from $x$ to $y$ up to homotopy fixing the endpoints.
- The conclusion: `Function.Bijective (cov.monodromy γ)`: the map `cov.monodromy γ`, which sends a point $e$ over $x$ to the endpoint of the lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, is injective and surjective onto the fibre over $y$.

This is the standard fact that path lifting identifies the fibres over two points joined by a path; the inverse map is transport along the reversed path. It concerns only the fibres over the two ends of $\gamma$, and says nothing about fibres over points in different path components.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$, monodromy along the class of a path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$ sends a point $e$ over $x$ to $\Gamma(1)$, for any continuous lift $\Gamma$ of $\gamma$ that starts at $e$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces. The map $p : E \to X$, the points $x, y$ of $X$, the path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$, the point $e$ of the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ and the continuous map $\Gamma : [0,1] \to E$ are implicit arguments.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over that point, which is discrete.
- `(hpΓ : p ∘ ⇑Γ = ⇑γ)`: $\Gamma$ lifts $\gamma$: $p(\Gamma(t)) = \gamma(t)$ for every $t \in [0,1]$.
- `(Γ_0 : Γ 0 = ↑e)`: the lift starts at $e$.
- The conclusion: monodromy along the homotopy class `Path.Homotopic.Quotient.mk γ` of $\gamma$, applied to $e$, is a point of the fibre over $y$; seen as a point of $E$, it is $\Gamma(1)$.

This is how monodromy, or translation of fibres, is defined in the literature: lift the path from $e$ and take the endpoint. By unique path lifting, $\Gamma$ is the only such lift. No condition on $\Gamma(1)$ is needed, since $p(\Gamma(1)) = \gamma(1) = y$ already puts it in the fibre over $y$.

## What it says
For a covering map $p : E \to X$: if a class of paths in $E$ from a point $e_x$ over $x$ to a point $e_y$ over $y$ projects to the class $\gamma$ in $X$, then monodromy along $\gamma$ sends $e_x$ to $e_y$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces. The map $p$, the points $x, y$ of $X$, the class $\gamma$ of paths from $x$ to $y$, and the points `ex` of the fibre $p^{-1}(x)$ and `ey` of the fibre $p^{-1}(y)$ are implicit arguments.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over that point, which is discrete.
- `(Γ : Path.Homotopic.Quotient ↑ex ↑ey)`: a class $\Gamma$ of paths in $E$ from $e_x$ to $e_y$, up to homotopy fixing the endpoints.
- `(eq : Γ.map { toFun := p, continuous_toFun := ⋯ } = γ.cast ⋯ ⋯)`: the image of $\Gamma$ under $p$, the class of $p \circ \Gamma$, is $\gamma$. The `cast` only rewrites the endpoints $x$ and $y$ of $\gamma$ as $p(e_x)$ and $p(e_y)$, which they equal, so that both sides are classes of paths between the same points.
- The conclusion: `cov.monodromy γ ex = ey`: monodromy along $\gamma$ sends $e_x$ to $e_y$.

In the literature, transport along $\gamma$ sends $e_x$ to the endpoint of the lift of $\gamma$ that starts at $e_x$. A path from $e_x$ to $e_y$ whose projection lies in the class of $\gamma$ is, by the lifting of homotopies, such a lift up to homotopy, so its endpoint $e_y$ is the transport of $e_x$. Equality of classes suffices, since monodromy depends only on homotopy classes.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the map $p : E \to X$ and the points $x, y, z$ of $X$ are implicit arguments.
- `(cov : IsCoveringMap p)`: $p$ is a covering map: each point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose preimage is homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U$ times the fibre over that point, which is discrete.
- `(γ : Path.Homotopic.Quotient x y)`: a class $\gamma$ of paths from $x$ to $y$, up to homotopy fixing the endpoints.
- `(γ' : Path.Homotopic.Quotient y z)`: a class $\gamma'$ of paths from $y$ to $z$.
- `(e : ↑(p ⁻¹' {x}))`: a point $e$ of the fibre over $x$.
- The conclusion: `cov.monodromy (γ.trans γ') e = cov.monodromy γ' (cov.monodromy γ e)`. Transporting $e$ along $\gamma$ followed by $\gamma'$, the class `γ.trans γ'`, gives the same point as transporting it along $\gamma$ to the fibre over $y$, then along $\gamma'$ to the fibre over $z$.

This is the functoriality of translation of fibres in the literature, covariant in the order in which the paths are traversed: the lift of a concatenation is the concatenation of the lifts, the second starting where the first ends.

## References and tests
- [§3.3 p.23, fiber translation functor](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/CONCISE/ConciseRevised.pdf) — the functor from the fundamental groupoid to sets given by translation of fibres.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `γ.trans γ'` traverses $\gamma$ first and $\gamma'$ second, as concatenation does in the literature, and on fibres it acts in the order of travel.
- Mathlib's fundamental group multiplies loops in the opposite order, the product $\gamma \delta$ being $\delta$ followed by $\gamma$; this lemma is stated with `trans`, so that convention does not enter here.
- `↑(p ⁻¹' {x})` is the fibre over $x$ taken as a type, a subtype of $E$.
- Mathlib's covering maps need not be surjective, so the fibre over $x$ may be empty; then there is no $e$ to transport.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.
