## What it says
For a function $f : E \to X$ between topological spaces and a set $s \subseteq X$, `IsCoveringMapOn f s` says that every point of $s$ is evenly covered by $f$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(f : E → X)`: a function from $E$ to $X$, with no continuity assumed.
- `(s : Set X)`: a set of points of $X$.
- The value: `∀ x ∈ s, IsEvenlyCovered f x (f ⁻¹' {x})`. For each $x \in s$, the fibre $f^{-1}(x)$ is discrete in the topology it inherits from $E$, and $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $X$ such that $f^{-1}(U)$ is open in $E$ and there is a homeomorphism $f^{-1}(U) \cong U \times f^{-1}(x)$ under which $f$ becomes the projection to $U$. So the preimage of $U$ is a disjoint union of open sheets, one for each point of the fibre over $x$, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$ by $f$.

For $s = X$ this is the definition of a covering map by evenly covered neighbourhoods, as in the literature. For a smaller $s$ it asks for this only at the points of $s$, with neighbourhoods open in $X$ and not merely in $s$; so it asks more than that the restriction $f^{-1}(s) \to s$ be a covering map.

## References and tests
- [§1.3 p.56, evenly covered neighborhoods](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf) — the definition of a covering space by evenly covered open neighbourhoods, which this asks for at the points of $s$.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- No continuity of $f$ is assumed, so the openness of $f^{-1}(U)$ is part of the condition; with it, $f$ is continuous on $f^{-1}(U)$. Nothing is said about $f$ away from these preimages, and for $s = \emptyset$ the condition holds for every $f$.
- Fibres may be empty: a point of $s$ outside the image of $f$ is evenly covered when it has an open neighbourhood that $f$ misses, with no sheets. So no surjectivity is required.
- `f ⁻¹' {x}` is the fibre over $x$, a set of points of $E$, taken as a type with the subspace topology; it indexes the sheets.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
If every point of a set $s \subseteq X$ is evenly covered by $f : E \to X$, then $f$, restricted to a map $f^{-1}(s) \to s$, is a covering map.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the function $f : E \to X$ is an implicit argument, with no continuity assumed.
- `(s : Set X)`: a set of points of $X$, not assumed open.
- `(hf : IsCoveringMapOn f s)`: every point $x$ of $s$ is evenly covered by $f$: its fibre is discrete, and it has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $X$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open in $E$ and homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U \times f^{-1}(x)$.
- The conclusion: `IsCoveringMap (s.restrictPreimage f)`. The map `s.restrictPreimage f` sends a point $e$ of $f^{-1}(s)$ to $f(e)$, a point of $s$. With the subspace topologies on $f^{-1}(s)$ and on $s$, it is a covering map: each point of $s$ has a neighbourhood in $s$ evenly covered by it.

This is the standard fact that a covering restricts to a covering over any subspace of the base, here with the hypothesis asked only over $s$: the sheets over $U$ cut down to sheets over $U \cap s$.

## References and tests
- [§1.3 Exercise 1, p.79](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf) — the restriction of a covering space to the preimage of a subspace of the base is a covering space.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `s.restrictPreimage f` is a function between subtypes: from $f^{-1}(s)$, as a type, to $s$, as a type, each with the subspace topology.
- Mathlib's covering maps need not be surjective, so the conclusion does not say that every point of $s$ is hit; points of $s$ outside the image of $f$ are allowed.
- $s$ may be any set, not open or empty; for $s = \emptyset$ both types are empty and the conclusion holds trivially.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
If every point of a set $s \subseteq X$ is evenly covered by $f : E \to X$, then so is every point of any subset $t \subseteq s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the function $f : E \to X$ and the sets $s, t \subseteq X$ are implicit arguments.
- `(hf : IsCoveringMapOn f s)`: every point $x$ of $s$ is evenly covered by $f$: its fibre is discrete, and it has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $X$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open in $E$ and homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U \times f^{-1}(x)$.
- `(ht : t ⊆ s)`: $t$ is contained in $s$.
- The conclusion: `IsCoveringMapOn f t`: every point of $t$ is evenly covered by $f$.

The condition is asked point by point, so it passes to fewer points, with the same neighbourhoods; $f$ itself is neither changed nor restricted. The inclusion goes the expected way: the condition on a larger set gives it on a smaller one.

## References and tests
- [§1.3 p.56, pointwise neighborhood condition](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf) — the definition of a covering space by an evenly covered neighbourhood of each point, the condition that this lemma passes to subsets.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsCoveringMapOn f s` asks for neighbourhoods open in $X$, not merely in $s$, and assumes no continuity of $f$; neither changes in passing from $s$ to $t$.
- For $t = \emptyset$ the conclusion holds for every $f$, so the lemma says nothing new there.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
If $s \subseteq X$ is open, $f^{-1}(s)$ is open in $E$, and the restriction $f^{-1}(s) \to s$ of $f$ is a covering map, then every point of $s$ is evenly covered by $f$ itself.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the function $f : E \to X$ is an implicit argument, with no continuity assumed.
- `(s : Set X)`: a set of points of $X$.
- `(hs : IsOpen s)`: $s$ is open in $X$.
- `(hfs : IsOpen (f ⁻¹' s))`: its preimage $f^{-1}(s)$ is open in $E$.
- `(hf : IsCoveringMap (s.restrictPreimage f))`: the map $f^{-1}(s) \to s$, $e \mapsto f(e)$, is a covering map for the subspace topologies.
- The conclusion: `IsCoveringMapOn f s`: each point $x$ of $s$ has a discrete fibre and an open neighbourhood $U$ in $X$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open in $E$ and homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U \times f^{-1}(x)$.

This is the converse of restricting a covering to the preimage of a subspace, for an open subspace. The two openness hypotheses turn neighbourhoods open in $s$ and in $f^{-1}(s)$ into neighbourhoods open in $X$ and in $E$. Since $f$ is not assumed continuous, the openness of $f^{-1}(s)$ does not follow from that of $s$, and it is asked for separately.

## References and tests
- [§1.3 p.56, neighborhood definition](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf) — the definition of a covering space by evenly covered open neighbourhoods, recovered here from the restriction to an open set.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `s.restrictPreimage f` is a function between subtypes, from $f^{-1}(s)$ to $s$, each a type with the subspace topology.
- `IsOpen (f ⁻¹' s)` would follow from `hs` if $f$ were continuous; it is assumed because nothing here makes $f$ continuous.
- Mathlib's covering maps need not be surjective, so neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion asks $f$ to map onto $s$.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
For the $n$-th cyclotomic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$, an inclusion-preserving bijection between the intermediate fields of $K/\mathbb{Q}$ and the subgroups of the group of Dirichlet characters modulo $n$ with values in a ring $R$.

- `(n : ℕ)`: the level, a natural number.
- `[NeZero n]`: $n \neq 0$.
- `[Field K] [NumberField K] [hK : IsCyclotomicExtension {n} ℚ K]`: $K$ is a number field that contains a primitive $n$-th root of unity and is generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by $n$-th roots of unity, so $K$ is $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ up to isomorphism.
- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, where the characters take their values.
- `[HasEnoughRootsOfUnity R (Monoid.exponent (ZMod n)ˣ)]`: for $m$ the exponent of $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$, $R$ has a primitive $m$-th root of unity and its $m$-th roots of unity form a cyclic group of order $m$; $R = \mathbb{C}$ will do.
- `[IsAbelianGalois ℚ K]`: $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with abelian Galois group.
- The value: an order isomorphism `IntermediateField ℚ K ≃o Subgroup (DirichletCharacter R n)`, both sides ordered by inclusion. It composes the Galois correspondence, which reverses inclusion, with `subgroupGalEquivSubgroupChar n K R`, which reverses it too, between subgroups of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$ and subgroups of characters; the two reversals cancel. A field $F$ goes to the characters trivial on $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, an automorphism being read as a unit modulo $n$: the characters of $\mathrm{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$.

This is the classical correspondence between subfields of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and groups of Dirichlet characters modulo $n$. The level $n$ need not be the conductor of $F$: a character of smaller modulus dividing $n$ appears as the character modulo $n$ it induces.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB [`nf.dirichlet_group`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/nf/nf.dirichlet_group) — the group of Dirichlet characters of an abelian number field, which corresponds to the image of the field here when $n$ is its conductor.
- `IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.mem_intermediateFieldEquivSubgroupChar_iff` — passes: a character $\chi$ lies in the subgroup attached to $F$ exactly when $\chi(\sigma) = 1$ for every $\sigma$ in the fixing subgroup of $F$, read as a unit modulo $n$.

The test pins down which subgroup each field gets, the characters trivial on $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, and so fixes the direction of the bijection.

## Lean subtleties
- `DirichletCharacter R n` is Mathlib's group of multiplicative characters of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ with values in $R$, which send non-units to $0$; they need not be primitive.
- `[NumberField K]` and `[IsAbelianGalois ℚ K]` hold for every $n$-th cyclotomic field, so they do not narrow the statement.
- An automorphism $\sigma$ is read as the unit $a$ modulo $n$ with $\sigma(\zeta) = \zeta^a$ for every $n$-th root of unity $\zeta$; no choice of $\zeta$ is involved.
- For $n = 1$ or $n = 2$, $K = \mathbb{Q}$ and both sides have one element.

## What it says
For a commutative ring $R$, the type of nonzero prime ideals of $R$; for a Dedekind domain, these are its primes of height one.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with $1$; the explicit argument `R` is its underlying type.
- The fields: a point of `HeightOneSpectrum R` consists of an ideal `asIdeal` of $R$, a proof `isPrime` that it is a prime ideal, and a proof `ne_bot` that it is not the zero ideal $\bot$. By the `@[ext]` attribute, two points are equal when their ideals are, so the type is the set of nonzero prime ideals of $R$.

For a Dedekind domain, the setting of the docstring, the nonzero primes are exactly the primes of height one and, unless $R$ is a field, exactly the maximal ideals. For the ring of integers of a number field they are its finite primes.

## References and tests
The notion is the standard one: the nonzero prime ideals of $R$, which for the ring of integers of a number field are its finite primes.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- The structure asks only that $R$ be a commutative ring, not a Dedekind domain. Over a general ring a nonzero prime need not have height one: in $k[x, y]$ the prime $(x, y)$ has height two, and in a ring that is not a domain a nonzero prime may have height zero. The results about it assume `IsDedekindDomain R`, where the name is accurate.
- `isPrime` excludes the whole ring, as prime ideals in the literature do; `ne_bot` excludes $0$, which is prime exactly when $R$ is a domain.
- If $R$ is a field, its only prime is $0$ and the type is empty; Mathlib counts fields as Dedekind domains, so this case arises. The docstring's remark that the type is the maximal spectrum is made for Krull dimension one, which excludes fields.
- `Type u_1` records a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
For a Dedekind domain $R$ with fraction field $K$ and a nonzero prime $v$ of $R$, the completion $K_v$ of $K$ at $v$.

- `[CommRing R] [IsDedekindDomain R]`: $R$ is a Dedekind domain; $R$ is an implicit argument.
- `[Field K] [Algebra R K] [IsFractionRing R K]`: $K$ is a field with a ring map from $R$ that makes it a fraction field of $R$.
- `(v : HeightOneSpectrum R)`: a nonzero prime ideal $v$ of $R$.
- The fields: one field, `toCompletion`, an element of `(v.valuation K).Completion`, the completion of $K$ for the uniform structure defined by its $v$-adic valuation; the constructor `ofCompletion` wraps such an element. So the type is a copy of that completion under a name of its own.

This is the standard completion $K_v$: the $v$-adic valuation makes $x \in K$ small when it is divisible by a high power of $v$, and $K_v$ is the completion of $K$ for the topology this defines. With $R$ the ring of integers of a number field, it is the completion at a finite prime.

## References and tests
The notion is the standard one: the completion of $K$ for its $v$-adic topology, which for a number field is its completion at a finite prime.

- `IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.denseRange_algebraMap` — passes: the image of $K$ in its completion at $v$, under the algebra map, is dense.

The test confirms a defining property of a completion, that $K$ sits densely in it, so the type is a completion of $K$ and not some larger field.

## Lean subtleties
- The valuation takes values in $\mathbb{Z}$ with a zero adjoined, written multiplicatively, rather than in the real numbers as an absolute value; both give the same topology on $K$, hence the same completion.
- The one-field structure is bookkeeping: it gives the completion a type of its own, and imposes no condition and identifies nothing.
- `Type u_2` records a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
For a Dedekind domain $R$ with fraction field $K$ and a nonzero prime $v$ of $R$, the $v$-adic valuation on $K$, written multiplicatively.

- `[CommRing R] [IsDedekindDomain R]`: $R$ is a Dedekind domain; $R$ is an implicit argument.
- `[Field K] [Algebra R K] [IsFractionRing R K]`: $K$ is a field with a ring map from $R$ that makes it a fraction field of $R$.
- `(v : HeightOneSpectrum R)`: a nonzero prime ideal $v$ of $R$.
- The value: a valuation on $K$ with values in `WithZero (Multiplicative ℤ)`, the elements $\exp(n)$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, of a multiplicative copy of $\mathbb{Z}$, with a $0$ adjoined below them. It extends `v.intValuation`, the $v$-adic valuation of $R$, to $K$ by `extendToLocalization`: for $x = r/s$ with $r, s \in R$ and $s \neq 0$, the value is $v(r)/v(s)$, as the docstring says. The proof passed to it shows that nonzero elements of $R$ have nonzero value, so the quotient makes sense.

On $R$, the value of $r \neq 0$ is $\exp(-n)$ when $v^n$ is the exact power of $v$ dividing the ideal $(r)$, and $0$ has value $0$. On $K$ the exponent is $-\mathrm{ord}_v(x)$, with $\mathrm{ord}_v(r/s) = \mathrm{ord}_v(r) - \mathrm{ord}_v(s)$. This is the standard $v$-adic valuation in multiplicative form: elements divisible by high powers of $v$ are small.

## References and tests
The notion is the standard one: the $v$-adic valuation of the fraction field of a Dedekind domain, from which its completion at $v$ is built.

- `IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation_of_algebraMap` — passes: on an element $r$ of $R$, seen in $K$, the valuation equals the $v$-adic valuation of $r$ in $R$.

The test checks that the valuation on $K$ restricts to the one on $R$, so the extension to fractions is the intended one.

## Lean subtleties
- Mathlib's valuations are multiplicative: a value $\exp(-n)$ in `WithZero (Multiplicative ℤ)`, written `ℤᵐ⁰` in the source, stands for the additive valuation $n$. The order is reversed relative to $\mathrm{ord}_v$, and the value $0$ of $0$ stands for $\mathrm{ord}_v(0) = \infty$.
- The value does not depend on the fraction $r/s$ chosen for $x$; the docstring's "chosen" describes the formula, not a choice the definition makes.
- `↑r` in the test is $r$ seen in $K$ through the algebra map.
- `Type u_2` records a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A map $i : \alpha \to \beta$ of topological spaces is dense inducing when the topology of $\alpha$ is the one induced by $i$ from $\beta$ and the image of $i$ is dense in $\beta$.

- `[TopologicalSpace α] [TopologicalSpace β]`: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are topological spaces.
- `(i : α → β)`: a function from $\alpha$ to $\beta$.
- `extends Topology.IsInducing i`: the first field says that $i$ is inducing: the open sets of $\alpha$ are exactly the preimages $i^{-1}(V)$ of the open sets $V$ of $\beta$.
- The field `dense : DenseRange i`: the range $i(\alpha)$ is dense in $\beta$, that is, its closure is all of $\beta$.

These are the two standard conditions on a map along which functions can be extended by continuity, the inclusion of a dense subspace being the model case. Injectivity is not asked: an inducing map identifies only points that the topology of $\alpha$ cannot separate, so it is injective when $\alpha$ is $T_0$, and the injective version is a dense embedding.

## References and tests
- [Semmes Def.1.3.1; §1.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — density and the induced topology.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- The structure is a proposition: it holds or fails, and carries no data.
- `extends` means that `IsDenseInducing i` consists of the fields of `Topology.IsInducing i` together with the field `dense`; a dense inducing map can be used wherever an inducing one is asked for.
- Continuity of $i$ is not listed, but follows from its being inducing.
- If $\alpha$ is empty, the range is empty, which is dense only in the empty space; so a map from the empty space is dense inducing only into the empty space.
- `[TopologicalSpace α]` and `[TopologicalSpace β]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
For a dense inducing map $i : \alpha \to \beta$, the closure of the image of a neighbourhood of a point $a$ is a neighbourhood of $i(a)$.

- `[TopologicalSpace α] [TopologicalSpace β]`: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are topological spaces; the map $i$, the set $s \subseteq \alpha$ and the point $a \in \alpha$ are implicit arguments.
- `(di : IsDenseInducing i)`: $i$ is dense inducing: $\alpha$ carries the topology induced by $i$, and $i(\alpha)$ is dense in $\beta$.
- `(hs : s ∈ nhds a)`: $s$ is a neighbourhood of $a$: it contains an open set containing $a$.
- The conclusion: `closure (i '' s) ∈ nhds (i a)`: the closure of $i(s)$ in $\beta$ is a neighbourhood of $i(a)$.

The reason is short. Since the topology of $\alpha$ is induced, $s$ contains $i^{-1}(V)$ for some open $V \ni i(a)$; since $i(\alpha)$ is dense, the open set $V$ lies in the closure of $V \cap i(\alpha)$, which is contained in $i(s)$. The closure is needed: for the inclusion of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the image of a neighbourhood of $0$ is a set of rationals, never a neighbourhood in $\mathbb{R}$.

## References and tests
- [Semmes Def.1.3.1; §1.5](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — density and the induced topology, the two facts the argument uses.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `nhds a` is the filter of neighbourhoods of $a$; `s ∈ nhds a` says that $s$ is a neighbourhood of $a$, not necessarily open.
- `i '' s` is the image $i(s)$, and `closure` is taken in $\beta$.
- `[TopologicalSpace α]` and `[TopologicalSpace β]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
Given a dense inducing map $i : \alpha \to \beta$ and a function $f : \alpha \to \gamma$, the candidate extension of $f$ to $\beta$: at $b \in \beta$, a limit of $f(a)$ as $i(a)$ tends to $b$.

- `[TopologicalSpace α] [TopologicalSpace β]`: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are topological spaces; the map $i : \alpha \to \beta$ is an implicit argument.
- `[TopologicalSpace γ]`: $\gamma$ is a topological space, where $f$ takes its values.
- `(di : IsDenseInducing i)`: $i$ is dense inducing: $\alpha$ carries the topology induced by $i$, and $i(\alpha)$ is dense in $\beta$.
- `(f : α → γ)`: any function, not assumed continuous.
- `(b : β)`: the point of $\beta$ at which the extension is evaluated.
- The value: `limUnder (comap i (𝓝 b)) f`, a limit of $f$ along the filter `comap i (𝓝 b)`, which is generated by the preimages $i^{-1}(V)$ of the neighbourhoods $V$ of $b$. If $f$ has a limit along it, the value is such a limit; if not, it is an unspecified point of $\gamma$.

As the docstring says, if $\gamma$ is Hausdorff and $f$ has a continuous extension to $\beta$, that extension is unique and is this function; in general this function need not be continuous, nor even agree with $f$. Classically the extension by continuity is defined when these limits exist and are unique; this definition is total, and agrees with it there.

## References and tests
- [Semmes §§7.1.5,7.2.1](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf).

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- `limUnder` uses classical choice: it picks a limit when one exists, and some point otherwise. These junk values lie outside the case the docstring describes.
- If $\gamma$ is not Hausdorff, a limit need not be unique, and which one is taken is arbitrary.
- At a point $i(a)$, the filter `comap i (𝓝 (i a))` is the neighbourhood filter of $a$, since $\alpha$ carries the induced topology. So the value there is a limit of $f$ at $a$, which is $f(a)$ when $\gamma$ is Hausdorff and $f$ is continuous at $a$.
- `𝓝 b` is the filter of neighbourhoods of $b$, and `comap i` pulls a filter on $\beta$ back to $\alpha$.
- `f (di.dense.some b)` is a value of $f$ at a point that density provides; it serves only to show that $\gamma$ is nonempty, which `limUnder` needs.

## What it says
A subset $t$ of a fibre $f^{-1}(x)$ is discrete if, at each point of $t$, $f$ is the function of an open partial homeomorphism whose source contains that point.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; the set $t \subseteq E$ and the point $x \in X$ are implicit arguments.
- `(f : E → X)`: a function from $E$ to $X$.
- `(htx : t ⊆ f ⁻¹' {x})`: every point of $t$ lies over $x$.
- `(hf : ∀ e ∈ t, ∃ (φ : OpenPartialHomeomorph E X), e ∈ φ.source ∧ ↑φ = f)`: for every $e \in t$ there is an open partial homeomorphism $\varphi$ from $E$ to $X$, a homeomorphism from an open set of $E$, its source, onto an open set of $X$, whose source contains $e$ and whose underlying function is $f$.
- The conclusion: `IsDiscrete t`: the topology that $t$ inherits from $E$ is discrete, so every point of $t$ is open in $t$.

The reason is the usual one: $f$ is injective on the source of $\varphi$, an open neighbourhood of $e$, so that neighbourhood meets $t \subseteq f^{-1}(x)$ only in $e$. This is the argument that the fibres of a local homeomorphism are discrete.

## References and tests
- [Proof, discrete-fiber argument before choosing disjoint sheets](https://www.matem.unam.mx/~omar/notes/propetale.html) — the argument that the fibres are discrete, made before the disjoint sheets are chosen.

No test is recorded.

## Lean subtleties
- An `OpenPartialHomeomorph E X` comes with a function defined on all of $E$, which is a homeomorphism only from its open source onto its open target; `↑φ = f` asks that this function be $f$ everywhere, not only on the source.
- `IsDiscrete t` is a property of the set $t$ with its subspace topology; it says nothing about $t$ being finite or closed in $E$.
- $t = \emptyset$ is allowed, and is discrete.
- `[TopologicalSpace E]` and `[TopologicalSpace X]` are typeclass arguments: Lean finds the topologies by itself.

## What it says
A domain is a nontrivial semiring in which multiplication by a nonzero element can be cancelled, on the left and on the right.

- `[Semiring α]`: a semiring structure on the type `α`: addition and multiplication with $0$ and $1$, with multiplication not assumed commutative and no subtraction assumed.
- The parents: `IsCancelMulZero α`, that $ab = ac$ implies $b = c$ when $a \neq 0$, and $ab = cb$ implies $a = c$ when $b \neq 0$; and `Nontrivial α`, that `α` has two distinct elements, so that $0 \neq 1$.

As the docstring says, an integral domain is a commutative ring with this property, written `[CommRing α] [IsDomain α]`. In a ring, cancellation by nonzero elements is equivalent, by subtraction, to having no zero divisors ($ab = 0$ implies $a = 0$ or $b = 0$); so for commutative rings this is the usual definition of an integral domain, and for other rings that of a domain. For semirings cancellation is the stronger condition, and it is the one asked.

- `Nontrivial` excludes the zero ring, as the domains of the literature do.
- No commutativity is assumed: noncommutative domains, such as the real quaternions, are domains here.
- `Type u` records a universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A point $x$ of $X$ is evenly covered by $f : E \to X$, with sheets indexed by a discrete space $I$, when some open neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ has a preimage homeomorphic, over $U$, to $U \times I$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(f : E → X)`: a function, with no continuity assumed.
- `(x : X)`: the point.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: a topology on the explicit type `I`, which indexes the sheets.
- The value: `I` has the discrete topology, and there is a set $U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$, $U$ open, $f^{-1}(U)$ open in $E$, and a homeomorphism $H : f^{-1}(U) \cong U \times I$ whose first coordinate is $f$: $H(e) = (f(e), \cdot)$ for every $e \in f^{-1}(U)$.

Since $I$ is discrete, $U \times I$ is the disjoint union of the open copies $U \times \{i\}$ of $U$, so this says that $f^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$ by $f$: the evenly covered neighbourhood of the literature, with its sheets indexed by $I$. Restricting $H$ to the fibre over $x$ shows that $I$ is then homeomorphic to $f^{-1}(x)$.

- Because $f$ is not assumed continuous, the openness of $f^{-1}(U)$ is asked for separately; with it, $f$ is continuous on $f^{-1}(U)$.
- $I$ may be empty: then $f^{-1}(U)$ is empty, and $x$ is evenly covered, with no sheets, by a neighbourhood that $f$ misses.
- In the value, the inner `∀ x` ranges over the points of $f^{-1}(U)$, reusing the name $x$; `(H x).1.1` is the first coordinate of $H(x)$, a point of $U$, seen as a point of $X$.
- `≃ₜ` denotes a homeomorphism, and `f ⁻¹' U` the preimage $f^{-1}(U)$, taken as a type with the subspace topology.
- The docstring's remark explains why a simpler definition through trivializations is not used: it fails when $E$ is nonempty but $f$ has empty fibres. It does not change the meaning.

## What it says
If the point $x$ of $X$ is evenly covered by the map $f : E \to X$ with fibre $I$, this gives a homeomorphism from $I$ onto the fibre $f^{-1}(x)$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces; $f : E \to X$ is any map between them and $x$ is a point of $X$.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: $I$, the model fibre, is a topological space.
- `(h : IsEvenlyCovered f x I)`: $x$ is evenly covered by $f$ with fibre $I$. As the value unpacks it, this gives an open neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open, and a homeomorphism $H : f^{-1}(U) \cong U \times I$ whose first coordinate is $f$; the definition also asks that $I$ be discrete.
- The conclusion: `I ≃ₜ ↑(f ⁻¹' {x})`, a homeomorphism from $I$ onto the fibre $f^{-1}(x)$, with the subspace topology.

Its value sends $i \in I$ to $H^{-1}(x, i)$, which lies over $x$, and a point $e$ of the fibre to the $I$-coordinate of $H(e)$; both maps are continuous. This is the usual correspondence between the sheets over an evenly covered neighbourhood and the points of the fibre: each sheet $U \times \{i\}$ meets $f^{-1}(x)$ in exactly one point.

## What it says
If some neighbourhood of the point $x$ has empty preimage under $f : E \to X$, then $x$ is evenly covered by $f$ with an empty fibre $I$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces, and $f : E \to X$ is any map between them.
- `(I : Type u_3)`: the type $I$ that serves as the fibre.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: a topology on $I$.
- `[IsEmpty I]`: $I$ has no elements.
- `(hUx : U ∈ nhds x)`: the set $U \subseteq X$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, that is, it contains an open set containing $x$.
- `(hfU : f ⁻¹' U = ∅)`: no point of $E$ is mapped into $U$.
- The conclusion: `IsEvenlyCovered f x I`, the point $x$ is evenly covered by $f$ with fibre $I$: $I$ is discrete, and $x$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ with $f^{-1}(V)$ open and homeomorphic to $V \times I$ by a map whose first coordinate is $f$.

The hypotheses say that $x$ lies outside the closure of the image of $f$. Such a point is evenly covered, by a neighbourhood whose preimage is the union of no sheets; covering-space theory allows this, so a covering map need not be surjective. An empty fibre over $x$ alone would not be enough: for the inclusion of the open interval $(0,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}$, the point $0$ has an empty fibre, but every neighbourhood of it meets the image, so it is not evenly covered.

## What it says
A local trivialization of $f : E \to X$ with discrete fibre $I$ makes every point of its base set evenly covered by $f$, with fibre $I$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces, and $f : E \to X$ is any map between them.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: $I$, the fibre, is a topological space.
- `[DiscreteTopology I]`: its topology is discrete.
- The implicit `t : Bundle.Trivialization I f` is a local trivialization of $f$ with fibre $I$: an open set `t.baseSet` of $X$ and a homeomorphism from its preimage under $f$ onto the product of `t.baseSet` with $I$, whose first coordinate is $f$.
- `(hx : x ∈ t.baseSet)`: the point $x$ of $X$ lies in the base set of $t$.
- The conclusion: `IsEvenlyCovered f x I`, the point $x$ is evenly covered by $f$ with fibre $I$: $I$ is discrete, and $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open and homeomorphic to $U \times I$ by a map whose first coordinate is $f$.

Here $U$ can be taken to be the base set itself. This is the classical picture: when $I$ is discrete, $U \times I$ is the disjoint union of the open sheets $U \times \{i\}$, each mapped homeomorphically onto $U$, so a neighbourhood over which $f$ is trivial with discrete fibre is evenly covered in the usual sense.

## What it says
If $f : E \to s$ is a map into an open subset $s$ of $X$, and a point $x$ of $s$ is evenly covered by $f$ with fibre $I$, then $x$, as a point of $X$, is evenly covered with the same fibre by $f$ followed by the inclusion of $s$ into $X$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `(s : Set X)`: a subset $s$ of $X$, with the subspace topology.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: $I$, the fibre, is a topological space.
- `(hs : IsOpen s)`: $s$ is open in $X$.
- `(h : IsEvenlyCovered f x I)`: the point $x$ of $s$ is evenly covered by the map $f : E \to s$ with fibre $I$: $I$ is discrete, and $x$ has a neighbourhood $U$, open in $s$, with $f^{-1}(U)$ open and homeomorphic to $U \times I$ by a map whose first coordinate is $f$.
- The conclusion: `IsEvenlyCovered (Subtype.val ∘ f) (↑x) I`, the same with $f$ replaced by $f$ followed by the inclusion `Subtype.val` of $s$ into $X$, and $x$ seen as a point of $X$.

The same neighbourhood $U$ works: since $s$ is open, a set open in $s$ is open in $X$, and the preimage and the product homeomorphism are unchanged. The openness of $s$ is needed: for the one-point set $s = \{0\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and the map from a point onto it, $0$ is evenly covered in $s$, but not in $\mathbb{R}$, where the preimage of an open interval around $0$ is a single point rather than a copy of the interval.

## What it says
If the point $x$ is evenly covered by $f : E \to X$ with some fibre $I$, then it is evenly covered by $f$ with the actual fibre $f^{-1}(x)$ in the place of $I$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces, $f : E \to X$ is any map between them, and $x$ is a point of $X$.
- `[TopologicalSpace I]`: $I$ is a topological space.
- `(h : IsEvenlyCovered f x I)`: $x$ is evenly covered by $f$ with fibre $I$: $I$ is discrete, and $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ with $f^{-1}(U)$ open and homeomorphic to $U \times I$ by a map whose first coordinate is $f$.
- The conclusion: `IsEvenlyCovered f x ↑(f ⁻¹' {x})`, the same with $I$ replaced by the fibre $f^{-1}(x)$, with the subspace topology of $E$.

The model fibre $I$ is homeomorphic to the fibre over $x$, since each sheet $U \times \{i\}$ meets $f^{-1}(x)$ in exactly one point. Composing with that homeomorphism relabels the sheets by the points of the fibre, as the classical account names them; in particular the fibre is discrete in the subspace topology. The statement replaces the abstract index $I$ by one that $f$ and $x$ determine, though the matching of sheets with points still depends on the neighbourhood.

## What it says
`IsGalois F E` is the property that the field extension $E/F$ is Galois: separable and normal.

- `[Field F]`: $F$, the base, is a field.
- `[Field E]`: $E$ is a field.
- `[Algebra F E]`: $E$ is an algebra over $F$, through a ring homomorphism $F \to E$; since $F$ is a field this map is injective, so $E$ is a field extension of $F$.
- The class is a `Prop`: a property of the extension, not extra data.

Its two fields:

- `to_isSeparable : Algebra.IsSeparable F E`: $E/F$ is separable: every element of $E$ is algebraic over $F$, and its minimal polynomial is separable.
- `to_normal : Normal F E`: $E/F$ is normal: every element of $E$ is algebraic over $F$, and its minimal polynomial splits into linear factors over $E$.

This is the standard definition of a Galois extension as an algebraic, normal and separable one. It assumes no finiteness, so it covers infinite Galois extensions, as infinite Galois theory does; for finite extensions it agrees with the other usual definition, that the elements fixed by every $F$-automorphism of $E$ are exactly those of $F$.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB [`nf.is_galois`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/nf/nf.is_galois) — the LMFDB knowl on Galois number fields, which states the fixed-field characterisation.
- `IsGalois.fixedField_top` — passes: for a finite Galois extension, the field fixed by the group of all $F$-automorphisms of $E$ is the least intermediate field, the image of $F$.

The test proves, from this definition, one direction of the fixed-field characterisation that the knowl uses, so the normal-and-separable definition gives the expected Galois property for finite extensions, number fields among them.

- In Mathlib a separable extension is by definition algebraic, as the docstring says, and so is a normal one.
- `Type u_1` and `Type u_2` say that $F$ and $E$ are types, Lean's version of sets; the universe levels do not affect the mathematics.
- The extension is given by the map $F \to E$, not by an inclusion: $E$ need not contain $F$ literally.
- In the test, `⊥` is the least intermediate field, the image of $F$, not the zero field, and `⊤` is the whole automorphism group.
- The trivial extension $E = F$ is Galois.

## What it says
`IsHomeomorph f` says that the map $f : X \to Y$ between topological spaces is a homeomorphism.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces.
- `(f : X → Y)`: a function $f$ from $X$ to $Y$.
- The structure is a `Prop`: a property of $f$, not extra data.

Its three fields:

- `continuous : Continuous f`: $f$ is continuous.
- `isOpenMap : IsOpenMap f`: $f$ is open: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `bijective : Function.Bijective f`: $f$ is injective and surjective.

The usual definition asks for a bijection $f$ such that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are both continuous. For a bijection, the preimage of an open set $U$ under $f^{-1}$ is $f(U)$, so $f^{-1}$ is continuous exactly when $f$ is open, and the two definitions agree. As the docstring says, a continuous bijection alone would not do: the identity map from $\mathbb{R}$ with the discrete topology to $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology is a continuous bijection, but not a homeomorphism.

- `IsOpenMap f` is about images: open sets are sent to open sets. This is not continuity, which is about preimages.
- The topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, in square brackets: Lean finds them by itself. $X$ and $Y$ are types in the universes `u_1` and `u_2`, which do not affect the mathematics.
- When $X$ and $Y$ are both empty, the empty map is a homeomorphism, as it should be.

## What it says
A map $f : X \to Y$ that is a homeomorphism in the sense of `IsHomeomorph` is packaged as a bundled homeomorphism from $X$ to $Y$ whose forward map is $f$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces.
- `(f : X → Y)`: a function $f$ from $X$ to $Y$.
- `(hf : IsHomeomorph f)`: $f$ is continuous, open and bijective.
- The result: `X ≃ₜ Y`, a homeomorphism from $X$ to $Y$: a bijection together with its inverse, both continuous.

Its value takes as the underlying bijection $f$ with its inverse, built from the bijectivity of $f$. The forward map is continuous by `hf`, and the inverse is continuous because $f$ is open: the preimage of an open set $U$ under $f^{-1}$ is $f(U)$. This is the classical fact that a continuous open bijection is a homeomorphism, with $f^{-1}$ as inverse.

## What it says
`IsIntegral R x` says that the element $x$ of the $R$-algebra $A$ is integral over $R$: it is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with $1$.
- `[Ring A]`: $A$ is a ring with $1$, not necessarily commutative.
- `[Algebra R A]`: $A$ is an algebra over $R$, through a ring homomorphism $R \to A$, `algebraMap R A`, whose image commutes with every element of $A$.
- `(x : A)`: an element $x$ of $A$.

Its value, `(algebraMap R A).IsIntegralElem x`, says that there is a monic polynomial $p = X^n + a_{n-1}X^{n-1} + \dots + a_0$ in $R[X]$ with $p(x) = 0$ in $A$, the coefficients $a_i$ being carried into $A$ by the structure map.

This is the standard definition of an integral element, for algebras over a commutative ring; for $R = \mathbb{Z}$ and $A$ a number field it gives the algebraic integers. The polynomial must be monic: every element of a number field is a root of some nonzero integer polynomial, but $1/2 \in \mathbb{Q}$, for one, is the root of no monic one.

## What it says
An irreducible subset of a topological space is connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is a topological space, and $s$ is a subset of it.
- `(H : IsIrreducible s)`: $s$ is irreducible: it is nonempty, and any two open sets of $\alpha$ that both meet $s$ meet each other inside $s$. Equivalently, $s$ is nonempty and is not the union of two relatively closed subsets, neither of them all of $s$.
- The conclusion: `IsConnected s`, $s$ is connected: it is nonempty, and whenever two open sets of $\alpha$ cover $s$ and each meets $s$, they meet each other inside $s$.

This is the standard fact: a separation of $s$ into two disjoint nonempty relatively open pieces would give two open sets that both meet $s$ but not each other inside $s$, which irreducibility forbids. In the Stacks Project it comes right after the definition of irreducibility, with the same conventions: both notions ask for nonemptiness.

## What it says
`IsLeast s a` says that $a$ is a least element, a minimum, of the set $s$.

- `[LE α]`: a relation $\le$ on the type $\alpha$; nothing is assumed of it, not even that it is a partial order.
- `(s : Set α)`: a subset $s$ of $\alpha$.
- `(a : α)`: an element $a$ of $\alpha$.

Its value is `a ∈ s ∧ a ∈ lowerBounds s`: $a$ lies in $s$, and $a \le b$ for every $b \in s$.

This is the usual notion of a least element. It is stronger than being minimal, having no element of $s$ strictly below it, which in an order that is not total does not make an element lie below all the others; and unlike an infimum, $a$ must belong to $s$.

## What it says
`IsLeftCancelMulZero M₀` says that in $M_0$ every nonzero element can be cancelled on the left: if $a \neq 0$ and $ab = ac$, then $b = c$.

- `[Mul M₀] [Zero M₀]`: the type $M_0$ has a multiplication and an element $0$; nothing is assumed of them, not associativity, nor that $0$ absorbs products.
- The class is a `Prop`: a property of $M_0$, not extra data.

Its one field:

- `mul_left_cancel_of_ne_zero : ∀ {a : M₀}, a ≠ 0 → IsLeftRegular a`: every $a \neq 0$ is left regular, that is, the map $b \mapsto ab$ is injective.

This is the usual left cancellation law for nonzero elements. In a ring it amounts to having no nonzero zero divisors, since $ab = ac$ means $a(b - c) = 0$; for a commutative multiplication it is the same as cancellation on the right.

## What it says
`IsNormalClosure F K L` says that $L$ is a normal closure of the extension $K/F$: the minimal polynomial over $F$ of every element of $K$ splits in $L$, and $L$ is generated over $F$ by the roots of these polynomials.

Its two fields:

For an algebraic extension $K/F$ this makes $L$ a splitting field over $F$ of the minimal polynomials of the elements of $K$: the classical normal closure of $K/F$, up to isomorphism over $F$. For a finite separable extension, such as a number field over $\mathbb{Q}$, it is the Galois closure.

## What it says
In a locally path-connected space, an open set is connected if and only if it is path-connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: $X$ is a topological space, and $U$ is a subset of it.

A path-connected set is always connected; the converse is the standard fact for open subsets of locally path-connected spaces, such as open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or of a manifold: such a subset is itself locally path-connected, so its path components are open, and when it is connected there is only one. Openness cannot be dropped: in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the closed topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected.

## What it says

- `[Nonempty ι]`: the index type $\iota$ has an element.
- `[TopologicalSpace ι] [DiscreteTopology ι]`: $\iota$ carries the discrete topology.
- `(U : ι → Set E)`: the family of subsets $U_i$ of $E$.
- `(V : Set X)`: the base set $V \subseteq X$.
- `(open_V : IsOpen V)`: $V$ is open in $X$.
- `(open_iff : ∀ (i : ι) {W : Set X}, W ⊆ V → (IsOpen W ↔ IsOpen (f ⁻¹' W ∩ U i)))`: for each $i$ and each $W \subseteq V$, $W$ is open in $X$ if and only if $f^{-1}(W) \cap U_i$ is open in $E$.
- `(inj : ∀ (i : ι), Set.InjOn f (U i))`: $f$ is injective on each $U_i$.
- `(surj : ∀ (i : ι), Set.SurjOn f (U i) V)`: $V \subseteq f(U_i)$ for each $i$.
- `(disjoint : Pairwise (Function.onFun Disjoint U))`: $U_i \cap U_j = \emptyset$ whenever $i \neq j$.

The value is the trivialization whose map sends $e \in f^{-1}(V)$ to $(f(e), i)$, for the index $i$ with $e \in U_i$, and whose inverse sends $(x, i) \in V \times \iota$ to the point of $U_i$ over $x$; its source is $f^{-1}(V)$, its target $V \times \iota$, its base set $V$.

The hypotheses say that $V$ is evenly covered: $f^{-1}(V)$ is the disjoint union of the open sheets $U_i \cap f^{-1}(V)$, each mapped homeomorphically onto $V$, the condition that defines a covering space.

## What it says
The range of an open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces is an open subset of $Y$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument, not assumed continuous.
- `(hf : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- The conclusion: `IsOpen (Set.range f)`, the set $f(X) = \{f(x) \mid x \in X\}$ of values of $f$ is open in $Y$.

This is the image of the whole space $X$, which is open in $X$, so it is open in $Y$ by the definition of an open map; nothing more is assumed, as in the literature.

## References and tests
- [Semmes Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for open maps, the maps that send open sets to open sets.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `Set.range f` is the set of values of $f$, the image $f(X)$ of the whole domain; it is a subset of $Y$, and the statement says it is open in all of $Y$.
- `IsOpenMap f` asks only that $f$ send open sets to open sets; neither continuity nor surjectivity is assumed. For a surjective $f$ the statement says only that $Y$ is open.
- If $X$ is empty, the range is empty, hence open: the statement needs no exception.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.

## What it says
A continuous surjective open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces is a quotient map: $Y$ carries the quotient topology that $f$ induces from $X$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument.
- `(open_map : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(cont : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous: the preimage of every open subset of $Y$ is open in $X$.
- `(surj : Function.Surjective f)`: every point of $Y$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in X$.
- The conclusion: `Topology.IsQuotientMap f`, $f$ is surjective and a set $U \subseteq Y$ is open exactly when $f^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$.

This is the standard sufficient condition for a quotient map: continuity gives one direction; for the other, if $f^{-1}(U)$ is open, then so is its image, which is $U$ since $f$ is surjective. The three hypotheses are the usual ones, and each is needed.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for the quotient topology that a surjection induces.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- In Mathlib, `Topology.IsQuotientMap f` includes the surjectivity of $f$ along with the condition on open sets, as in the usual definition of a quotient map.
- `IsOpenMap f` does not include continuity, which is why `cont` is a hypothesis of its own.
- The converse fails: a quotient map need not be open. For example, the map from $[0, 1]$ to the circle that glues $0$ to $1$ is a quotient map, yet the image of the open set $[0, 1/2)$ is not open.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.
- If $X$ is empty, surjectivity forces $Y$ to be empty too, and the statement holds there with no exception.

## What it says
For maps $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ of topological spaces, if $f$ is continuous and surjective and the composite $g \circ f$ is open, then $g$ is open.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace Z]`: topologies on $X$, $Y$ and $Z$, which range over arbitrary types; the maps $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ are implicit arguments, and $g$ is not assumed continuous.
- `(hf : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous: the preimage of every open subset of $Y$ is open in $X$.
- `(f_surj : Function.Surjective f)`: every point of $Y$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in X$.
- `(h : IsOpenMap (g ∘ f))`: the composite $x \mapsto g(f(x))$ sends open subsets of $X$ to open subsets of $Z$.
- The conclusion: `IsOpenMap g`, the map $g$ sends open subsets of $Y$ to open subsets of $Z$.

This is the standard argument: for open $W \subseteq Y$, the preimage $f^{-1}(W)$ is open in $X$, and $(g \circ f)(f^{-1}(W)) = g(f(f^{-1}(W))) = g(W)$ since $f$ is surjective, so $g(W)$ is open.

## References and tests
- [Semmes Prop.2.7.9; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for the two notions of the argument, continuous maps and open maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `g ∘ f` applies $f$ first and then $g$, as $g \circ f$ does in the literature.
- `IsOpenMap` asks only that images of open sets be open; it includes no continuity, so the conclusion says nothing about the continuity of $g$.
- Surjectivity cannot be dropped: if $X$ is empty, then $g \circ f$ is open for every $g$, while $g$ need not be.
- The three topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.

## What it says
A map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces that has a continuous two-sided inverse $f' : Y \to X$ is an open map.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the maps $f : X \to Y$ and $f' : Y \to X$ are implicit arguments.
- `(h : Continuous f')`: the map $f'$ is continuous: the preimage under $f'$ of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(l_inv : Function.LeftInverse f f')`: $f(f'(y)) = y$ for every $y \in Y$.
- `(r_inv : Function.RightInverse f f')`: $f'(f(x)) = x$ for every $x \in X$.
- The conclusion: `IsOpenMap f`, the map $f$ sends open subsets of $X$ to open subsets of $Y$.

This is the standard fact that a bijection whose inverse is continuous is open: by the two identities, the image $f(U)$ of a set $U \subseteq X$ is its preimage $f'^{-1}(U)$, which is open when $U$ is, since $f'$ is continuous. Continuity of $f$ itself is not assumed, so $f$ need not be a homeomorphism.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for open maps and the continuity of inverse maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- Lean's names for the two identities read in the opposite order from what they ask of $f'$: `Function.LeftInverse f f'` says that $f$ is a left inverse of $f'$, that is $f \circ f' = \mathrm{id}_Y$, and `Function.RightInverse f f'` says that $f$ is a right inverse of $f'$, that is $f' \circ f = \mathrm{id}_X$. Together they say that $f$ is a bijection with inverse $f'$.
- `IsOpenMap f` asks only that $f$ send open sets to open sets; the statement says nothing about the continuity of $f$.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.
- Empty spaces need no exception: if $X$ is empty, so is $Y$, by the identities.

## What it says
A map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces is open if, at every point $x$, the image under $f$ of each neighbourhood of $x$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$; the statement says this with neighbourhood filters.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument, not assumed continuous.
- `(hf : ∀ (x : X), nhds (f x) ≤ Filter.map f (nhds x))`: for every $x \in X$, every set $T \subseteq Y$ whose preimage $f^{-1}(T)$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$. Equivalently, for every neighbourhood $s$ of $x$, the image $f(s)$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$.
- The conclusion: `IsOpenMap f`, the map $f$ sends open subsets of $X$ to open subsets of $Y$.

This is the standard pointwise criterion for an open map: if $U$ is open and $x \in U$, then $U$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, so $f(U)$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$; a set that is a neighbourhood of each of its points is open. The converse holds as well, so the hypothesis is no stronger than openness.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for open maps and neighbourhoods.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `nhds x`, written `𝓝 x` in the source, is the neighbourhood filter of $x$: the collection of all sets that contain an open set containing $x$, so its members need not be open.
- `Filter.map f (nhds x)` is the image filter: the sets $T \subseteq Y$ with $f^{-1}(T)$ a neighbourhood of $x$.
- Filters are ordered by reverse inclusion: $F \le G$ says that every member of $G$ is a member of $F$. So `nhds (f x) ≤ Filter.map f (nhds x)` says that every member of the image filter is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$, as read above, not the other way round.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.

## What it says
For a continuous open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces and any subset $s \subseteq Y$, taking preimages commutes with taking closures: $f^{-1}(\overline{s}) = \overline{f^{-1}(s)}$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument.
- `(hf : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(hfc : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous: the preimage of every open subset of $Y$ is open in $X$.
- `(s : Set Y)`: an arbitrary subset $s$ of $Y$.
- The conclusion: `f ⁻¹' closure s = closure (f ⁻¹' s)`, the preimage of the closure of $s$ equals the closure in $X$ of the preimage of $s$.

This is the standard fact for continuous open maps. Continuity gives $\overline{f^{-1}(s)} \subseteq f^{-1}(\overline{s})$, the right side being closed and containing $f^{-1}(s)$. Conversely, if $f(x) \in \overline{s}$ and $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$, then $f(U)$ is an open neighbourhood of $f(x)$, so it meets $s$, and $U$ meets $f^{-1}(s)$. Neither injectivity nor surjectivity is needed.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for closures, continuous maps and open maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `f ⁻¹' s` is Lean's notation for the preimage $f^{-1}(s)$, and `closure s` is the closure of $s$, the smallest closed set containing it.
- Both hypotheses matter. Without openness it fails for the map from a point to $\mathbb{R}$ with value $0$ and $s = (0, 1)$: the left side is the point and the right side is empty. Without continuity it fails for the identity from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ with the discrete topology, which is open, and $s = (0, 1)$.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.
- For empty $s$ both sides are empty, so the statement needs no exception.

## What it says
For a continuous injective open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces and a closed set $s \subseteq X$, the preimage of the closure of $f(s)$ is $s$ again: $f^{-1}(\overline{f(s)}) = s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument.
- `(h₁ : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(h₂ : Function.Injective f)`: $f$ is injective.
- `(h₃ : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous.
- `(s : Set X)`: a subset $s$ of $X$.
- `(hs' : IsClosed s)`: $s$ is closed in $X$.
- The conclusion: `f ⁻¹' closure (f '' s) = s`, the points of $X$ that $f$ sends into the closure of $f(s)$ are exactly the points of $s$.

It follows from the standard facts behind it: for a continuous open map, the preimage of a closure is the closure of the preimage, so the left side is $\overline{f^{-1}(f(s))}$; injectivity gives $f^{-1}(f(s)) = s$; and $\overline{s} = s$ as $s$ is closed.

## References and tests
- [Semmes §1.4.1; Def.2.8.3](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for closures and for open maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `f '' s` is Lean's notation for the image $f(s)$, `f ⁻¹' t` for the preimage $f^{-1}(t)$, and `closure t` is the smallest closed set containing $t$.
- The closure of $f(s)$ in $Y$ may contain points outside the range of $f$; taking the preimage discards them.
- Injectivity cannot be dropped: the map $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ from $\mathbb{R}$ onto the circle is continuous and open, and for $s = \{0\}$ the left side is the set of all multiples of $2\pi$.
- Without closedness, the same argument gives $\overline{s}$ on the right in place of $s$.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.

## What it says
For a continuous open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces and any subset $s \subseteq Y$, taking preimages commutes with taking boundaries: $f^{-1}(\partial s) = \partial f^{-1}(s)$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument.
- `(hf : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(hfc : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous: the preimage of every open subset of $Y$ is open in $X$.
- `(s : Set Y)`: an arbitrary subset $s$ of $Y$.
- The conclusion: `f ⁻¹' frontier s = frontier (f ⁻¹' s)`, the preimage of the boundary of $s$ equals the boundary in $X$ of the preimage of $s$.

This is the standard consequence of the corresponding fact for closures: the boundary of a set is the intersection of its closure with the closure of its complement; for a continuous open map, preimage commutes with closure, and preimage always commutes with intersections and complements. Neither injectivity, nor surjectivity, nor any separation axiom is needed.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for closures, boundaries, continuous maps and open maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `frontier s` is the boundary of $s$: its closure minus its interior, which equals $\overline{s} \cap \overline{Y \setminus s}$.
- `f ⁻¹' s` is Lean's notation for the preimage $f^{-1}(s)$.
- Both hypotheses matter, as for closures: for the map from a point to $\mathbb{R}$ with value $0$, which is continuous but not open, and $s = (0, 1)$, the left side is the point and the right side is empty.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.
- For empty $s$ both sides are empty, so the statement needs no exception.

## What it says
For a continuous open map $f : X \to Y$ of topological spaces and any subset $s \subseteq Y$, taking preimages commutes with taking interiors: $f^{-1}(\operatorname{int} s) = \operatorname{int} f^{-1}(s)$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types; the map $f : X \to Y$ is an implicit argument.
- `(hf₁ : IsOpenMap f)`: $f$ is an open map: the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.
- `(hf₂ : Continuous f)`: $f$ is continuous: the preimage of every open subset of $Y$ is open in $X$.
- `(s : Set Y)`: an arbitrary subset $s$ of $Y$.
- The conclusion: `f ⁻¹' interior s = interior (f ⁻¹' s)`, the preimage of the interior of $s$ equals the interior in $X$ of the preimage of $s$.

This is the standard fact for continuous open maps. Continuity makes $f^{-1}(\operatorname{int} s)$ an open subset of $f^{-1}(s)$, hence a subset of its interior. Conversely, $f(\operatorname{int} f^{-1}(s))$ is open, since $f$ is open, and lies in $s$, hence in $\operatorname{int} s$. Neither injectivity nor surjectivity is needed.

## References and tests
- [Semmes](https://math.rice.edu/~semmes/math443b.pdf) — notes cited for interiors, continuous maps and open maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `f ⁻¹' s` is Lean's notation for the preimage $f^{-1}(s)$, and `interior s` is the interior of $s$, the union of all open sets contained in it.
- Both hypotheses matter. Without openness it fails for the map from a point to $\mathbb{R}$ with value $0$ and $s = [0, 1)$: the left side is empty and the right side is the point. Without continuity it fails for the identity from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ with the discrete topology, which is open, and $s = [0, 1]$.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.
- For $s = Y$ both sides are all of $X$, and for empty $s$ both are empty.

## What it says
If $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Z \to W$ are open quotient maps of topological spaces, then so is their product $f \times g : X \times Z \to Y \times W$, $(x, z) \mapsto (f(x), g(z))$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace Z] [TopologicalSpace W]`: topologies on $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and $W$, which range over arbitrary types; the maps $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Z \to W$ are implicit arguments.
- `(hf : IsOpenQuotientMap f)`: $f$ is an open quotient map: surjective, continuous and open.
- `(hg : IsOpenQuotientMap g)`: $g$ is an open quotient map.
- The conclusion: `IsOpenQuotientMap (Prod.map f g)`, the map $(x, z) \mapsto (f(x), g(z))$ is surjective, continuous and open for the product topologies on $X \times Z$ and $Y \times W$.

This is the standard fact that open quotient maps are stable under finite products. Surjectivity and continuity pass to products directly. For openness, the image of an open rectangle $U \times V$ is $f(U) \times g(V)$, which is open, and every open set of $X \times Z$ is a union of such rectangles. Openness is what makes this work: the product of two quotient maps need not be a quotient map.

## References and tests
- [Wendl](https://www.math.hu-berlin.de/~wendl/Sommer2026/Topologie1/lecturenotes.pdf) — lecture notes on topology, for product topologies and quotient maps.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- In Mathlib, `IsOpenQuotientMap f` is the conjunction of three properties of $f$: surjective, continuous and open. Such a map is a quotient map: $Y$ carries the quotient topology from $X$.
- `Prod.map f g` is the map that applies $f$ to the first coordinate and $g$ to the second.
- The four topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, and Lean finds the topologies of `X × Z` and `Y × W` by itself: they are the product topologies.
- If $X$ or $Z$ is empty, surjectivity forces $Y$ or $W$ to be empty as well, so both products are empty and the statement holds with no exception.

## What it says
`IsOrderedRing R` says that a partial order on a semiring $R$ is compatible with its operations, which makes $R$ an ordered semiring. It is a proposition about the two structures, with no data of its own.

- `[Semiring R]`: a semiring structure on the type `R`: an associative addition and multiplication with $0$ and $1$, addition commutative and multiplication distributing over it; subtraction is not required.
- `[PartialOrder R]`: a partial order $\le$ on $R$.

It has no fields of its own; its conditions are those of the four classes it extends:

- `IsOrderedAddMonoid R`: addition is monotone: $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$ and $c + a \le c + b$.
- `ZeroLEOneClass R`: $0 \le 1$.
- `PosMulMono R`: multiplication on the left by a nonnegative element is monotone: $0 \le a$ and $b \le c$ imply $ab \le ac$.
- `MulPosMono R`: the same on the right: $0 \le a$ and $b \le c$ imply $ba \le ca$.

This is the notion of an ordered semiring, with a partial order rather than a total one, and with monotonicity on both sides, since multiplication need not be commutative. For a ring with a total order, the four conditions are equivalent to the usual axioms of an ordered ring: $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$, and $0 \le a$, $0 \le b$ imply $0 \le ab$.

## References and tests
No reference stating this definition in this generality is recorded for it.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- Despite its name, the class applies to semirings: no additive inverses are required, and $\mathbb{N}$ with its usual order is an example.
- It is a mixin: the semiring and the order are separate typeclass arguments, which Lean finds by itself, and the class adds only the conditions linking them. Being a `Prop`, it carries no data, so an instance chooses nothing.
- `ZeroLEOneClass R` is a condition of its own: for a partial order it does not follow from the other three, which all hold when $a \le b$ only for $a = b$. For a ring with a total order it does follow from them.
- In the zero semiring, where $0 = 1$, every condition holds.
- `Type u_1` says that $R$ is a type, Lean's version of a set; the universe level `u_1` does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A subset $F$ of a topological space $X$ is path connected when it contains a point from which every point of $F$ can be reached by a path that stays in $F$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on $X$, which ranges over arbitrary types.
- `(F : Set X)`: the subset $F$ of $X$ in question.

The value is `∃ x ∈ F, ∀ ⦃y⦄, y ∈ F → JoinedIn F x y`: there is a point $x \in F$ such that for every $y \in F$ there is a continuous $\gamma : [0, 1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, $\gamma(1) = y$ and $\gamma(t) \in F$ for all $t$.

This is the usual notion: since paths can be reversed and concatenated, it says that $F$ is nonempty and that any two of its points are joined by a path in $F$. A path in $X$ with values in $F$ is the same as a path in $F$ with its subspace topology, so it is the path-connectedness of the space $F$. It differs from the pairwise definition only at $F = \emptyset$, which that definition calls path connected and this one does not.

## References and tests
- [p.17, pairwise path-connectedness; p.19, reversal and concatenation](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf) — Hatcher's notes on point-set topology: path-connectedness as any two points joined by a path, and the reversal and concatenation of paths that make the two forms agree.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- Nonemptiness is built in: the empty set is not path connected here, as the empty set is not connected under Mathlib's `IsConnected`. The pairwise definition would make it path connected vacuously.
- `JoinedIn F x y` says that some path from $x$ to $y$, a continuous map from the unit interval $[0, 1]$ into $X$, takes all its values in $F$.
- `⦃y⦄` is a binder that Lean fills in by itself once the hypothesis `y ∈ F` is given; it does not change the meaning.
- The topology is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass: Lean finds it by itself, and $F$ carries no topology of its own, only the paths of $X$ that stay in it.
- The definition is a proposition: the point $x$ is asserted to exist, not chosen.

## What it says
The image of a path-connected set under a continuous map is path connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types.
- `(hF : IsPathConnected F)`: the set $F \subseteq X$, an implicit argument, is path connected: it contains a point that can be joined to every point of $F$ by a path staying in $F$; in particular $F$ is nonempty.
- `(hf : Continuous f)`: the map $f : X \to Y$, an implicit argument, is continuous.
- The conclusion: `IsPathConnected (f '' F)`, the image $f(F) \subseteq Y$ is path connected.

This is the standard fact that path-connectedness is preserved by continuous maps: if $\gamma$ is a path in $F$ from $x$ to $y$, then $f \circ \gamma$ is a path in $f(F)$ from $f(x)$ to $f(y)$. Surjectivity of $f$ is not needed, since the conclusion concerns only the image, and $f(F)$ is nonempty because $F$ is.

## References and tests
- [p.18, continuous-surjection proposition applied to the image; p.11, restrictions](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/Top/TopNotes.pdf) — Hatcher's notes on point-set topology: a continuous surjection carries path-connectedness to its target, applied here to the restriction of $f$ to $F$, onto $f(F)$.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `IsPathConnected` includes nonemptiness: the empty set is not path connected in Mathlib. The image of a nonempty set is nonempty, so this convention costs nothing here.
- `f '' F` is Lean's notation for the image $f(F)$ of a set.
- $f$ is asked to be continuous on all of $X$; continuity at the points of $F$, with respect to $F$, would be enough for the argument, as only the values of $f$ on paths in $F$ are used.
- The two topologies are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds them by itself.

## What it says
If a set $F$ is path connected and a map $f$ is continuous on $F$, then the image $f(F)$ is path connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and $Y$, which range over arbitrary types.
- `(hF : IsPathConnected F)`: the set $F \subseteq X$, an implicit argument, is path connected: it contains a point that can be joined to every point of $F$ by a path staying in $F$; in particular $F$ is nonempty.
- `(hf : ContinuousOn f F)`: the map $f : X \to Y$, an implicit argument, is continuous on $F$: its restriction to $F$, with the subspace topology, is continuous. Nothing is asked of $f$ off $F$.
- The conclusion: `IsPathConnected (f '' F)`, the image $f(F) \subseteq Y$ is path connected.

This is the standard fact that a continuous image of a path-connected space is path connected, applied to the restriction of $f$ to $F$: if $\gamma$ is a path in $F$ from $x$ to $y$, then $f \circ \gamma$ is continuous, since $\gamma$ stays in $F$, and is a path in $f(F)$ from $f(x)$ to $f(y)$. Surjectivity is not needed, and $f(F)$ is nonempty because $F$ is.

## References and tests
- [Definition 7.1, p.40, paths in a subspace](https://www.math.hu-berlin.de/~wendl/Sommer2026/Topologie1/lecturenotes.pdf) — lecture notes on topology by Wendl: paths in a subspace, from which the statement follows directly.
- [Example B.3, p.207, subspace topology](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/1F5CB46192122ED291D321A762FE4CE3/9781316514887apx2_206-212.pdf/basic_ideas_from_topology.pdf) — an appendix on basic ideas from topology: the subspace topology, for which the restriction of $f$ to $F$ is continuous.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `ContinuousOn f F` says that at each point $x \in F$, $f(y)$ tends to $f(x)$ as $y$ tends to $x$ within $F$. It is weaker than continuity of $f$ on all of $X$, which is a special case, and the values of $f$ outside $F$ play no part.

## What it says
A path-connected subset of a topological space is connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on $X$, which ranges over arbitrary types.
- `(hF : IsPathConnected F)`: the set $F \subseteq X$, an implicit argument, is path connected: it contains a point that can be joined to every point of $F$ by a path staying in $F$; in particular $F$ is nonempty.
- The conclusion: `IsConnected F`, the set $F$ is nonempty and cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty pieces, each cut out of $F$ by an open set of $X$; that is, $F$ with the subspace topology is a connected space.

This is the standard fact that path-connected spaces are connected: a separation of $F$ would pull back along a path between points of its two pieces to a separation of the interval $[0, 1]$, which is connected. The converse fails; the docstring points to the topologist's sine curve, the standard example of a connected set that is not path connected.

## What it says
In a topological space $X$, if a subset $F$ is path-connected, then any two points of $F$ can be joined by a path that stays inside $F$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: $X$ is a topological space; `X : Type u_1` is a type, Lean's version of a set, and $F$ is a subset of it.
- `(h : IsPathConnected F)`: the subset $F$ is path-connected.
- `(x : X)`: a point $x$ of $X$.
- The conclusion: if $x \in F$, then for every $y \in F$, `JoinedIn F x y` holds: there is a continuous path $\gamma : [0,1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, $\gamma(1) = y$ and $\gamma(t) \in F$ for every $t \in [0,1]$.

Path-connectedness of a subspace is usually defined in just this pairwise form: $F$ is nonempty and any two of its points are joined by a path in $F$. Mathlib's `IsPathConnected F` asks instead for one point of $F$ that is joined inside $F$ to every point of $F$; this theorem recovers the pairwise form, by running the path from that point to $x$ backwards and then the path from it to $y$. So the statement is the standard one, with no extra hypothesis and for every topological space.

A path-connected subset $F$ of a topological space $X$ lies inside the path component of any of its points.

## What it says
In a topological space $X$, the union of two path-connected sets that meet is path-connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: $X$ is a topological space; $U$ and $V$ are subsets of $X$.
- `(hU : IsPathConnected U)`: $U$ is path-connected: it is nonempty, and its points are joined to one another by paths lying in $U$.
- `(hV : IsPathConnected V)`: $V$ is path-connected in the same sense.
- `(hUV : (U ∩ V).Nonempty)`: $U$ and $V$ have a point in common.
- The conclusion: `IsPathConnected (U ∪ V)`, the union $U \cup V$ is path-connected.

This is the standard gluing fact: a common point $z$ of $U$ and $V$ is joined to every point of $U$ by a path in $U$ and to every point of $V$ by a path in $V$, and running one such path backwards and then another joins any two points of $U \cup V$ inside it. Neither set has to be open or closed, and the intersection need not be path-connected; the hypothesis that it is nonempty cannot be dropped, as two disjoint points show.

## What it says
A set $s$ in a topological space is preconnected when two open sets cannot split it: whenever two open sets cover $s$ and each meets $s$, they meet each other inside $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is a topological space; `α : Type u` is a type, Lean's version of a set.
- `(s : Set α)`: a subset $s$ of $\alpha$.
- The value: `IsPreconnected s` is the proposition that for all open subsets $u, v$ of $\alpha$ with $s \subseteq u \cup v$, $s \cap u \neq \emptyset$ and $s \cap v \neq \emptyset$, also $s \cap (u \cap v) \neq \emptyset$.

The sets $s \cap u$, for $u$ open in $\alpha$, are exactly the open sets of $s$ in the subspace topology, so the condition says that $s$ is not the union of two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets: $s$, with the subspace topology, is connected. The open sets $u$ and $v$ may meet outside $s$; only their traces on $s$ count. The one difference from the usual definition of a connected space is the empty set, which is preconnected here; connectedness proper, `IsConnected` in Mathlib, adds that the set is nonempty.

## What it says
In a topological space, the closure of a preconnected set is preconnected.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is a topological space, and $s$ is a subset of it.
- `(H : IsPreconnected s)`: $s$ is preconnected: two open sets of $\alpha$ that cover $s$ and each meet $s$ also meet each other inside $s$. Equivalently, $s$ with the subspace topology is connected or empty.
- The conclusion: `IsPreconnected (closure s)`, the closure $\overline{s}$ of $s$ in $\alpha$, the smallest closed set containing it, is preconnected too.

This is the classical fact that the closure of a connected set is connected. The argument is the usual one: an open set that meets $\overline{s}$ already meets $s$, so two open sets that split $\overline{s}$ would split $s$. Preconnectedness differs from connectedness only in allowing the empty set, and the closure of the empty set is empty, so nothing is lost or added.

## What it says
A map into a discrete space that is continuous on a preconnected set takes the same value at any two points of the set.

So $f$ is constant on $s$. The target is an arbitrary discrete space, not only the two-point space, which is the general form of the statement.

## What it says
On a preconnected set $s$, a symmetric and transitive relation that holds between each point and all nearby points of $s$ holds between any two points of $s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is a topological space, and $s$ is a subset of it.
- `(hs : IsPreconnected s)`: $s$ is preconnected: two open sets of $\alpha$ that cover $s$ and each meet $s$ also meet each other inside $s$. Equivalently, $s$ with the subspace topology is connected or empty.
- `(P : α → α → Prop)`: a binary relation $P$ on $\alpha$.
- `(h : ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ᶠ (y : α) in nhdsWithin x s, P x y)`: for each $x \in s$ there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ in $\alpha$ with $P(x, y)$ for every $y \in U \cap s$.
- `(h' : ∀ (x y z : α), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → z ∈ s → P x y → P y z → P x z)`: $P$ is transitive on $s$.
- `(h'' : ∀ (x y : α), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → P x y → P y x)`: $P$ is symmetric on $s$.
- `(hx : x ∈ s)` and `(hy : y ∈ s)`: $x$ and $y$ are points of $s$.
- The conclusion: $P(x, y)$.

This is the familiar principle that an equivalence relation on a connected space whose classes are open has a single class. Reflexivity is not assumed, since the first hypothesis gives $P(x, x)$. The usual proof applies: for fixed $x$, the points $y$ of $s$ with $P(x, y)$ form a nonempty subset of $s$ that is open and closed in $s$, hence all of $s$. Symmetry and transitivity are asked only on $s$, which is what this argument uses.

## What it says
In a $T_1$ space, a preconnected set with at least two points is infinite.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: $X$ is a topological space, and $s$ is a subset of it.
- `[T1Space X]`: $X$ is a $T_1$ space: its points are closed, equivalently, for any two distinct points each has a neighbourhood missing the other.
- `(h : IsPreconnected s)`: $s$ is preconnected: two open sets of $X$ that cover $s$ and each meet $s$ also meet each other inside $s$. Equivalently, $s$ with the subspace topology is connected or empty.
- `(hs : s.Nontrivial)`: $s$ has two distinct points.
- The conclusion: `s.Infinite`, the set $s$ is infinite.

This is the standard fact that a connected $T_1$ space with more than one point is infinite. The argument: a finite subset of a $T_1$ space is discrete in the subspace topology, since each of its points has a finite, hence closed, complement in it; and a discrete preconnected set has at most one point. The $T_1$ hypothesis cannot be dropped: the two-point Sierpiński space and the two-point indiscrete space are connected and finite.

## What it says
A preconnected set is discrete exactly when it has at most one point.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is a topological space, and $S$ is a subset of it.
- `(hS : IsPreconnected S)`: $S$ is preconnected: two open sets of $\alpha$ that cover $S$ and each meet $S$ also meet each other inside $S$. Equivalently, $S$ with the subspace topology is connected or empty.
- The conclusion: `IsDiscrete S ↔ S.Subsingleton`, the subspace topology on $S$ is discrete, every point of $S$ having a neighbourhood that meets $S$ in that point alone, if and only if $S$ has at most one point.

One direction is the familiar fact that a connected discrete space is a single point: if $S$ is discrete, any of its points is open and closed in $S$, so preconnectedness leaves no room for a second point. The other is immediate, since the empty set and a singleton carry only the discrete topology. Both sides concern the topology that $S$ inherits, not that of $\alpha$.
