- Countable includes finite: a compact space is σ-compact, and so is the empty space.
- As the docstring says, a covering sequence of compact sets can be extracted with `compactCovering`; the class itself only asserts that one exists, and fixes none.
- The docstring's note that a locally compact separable Hausdorff space need not be σ-compact is a remark about the notion, not part of the definition.
- `Type u_4` says that $X$ is a type, Lean's version of a set; the universe level does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
A topological space $X$ is simply connected when its fundamental groupoid is equivalent, as a category, to the category with one object and only its identity morphism.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type `X`.
- The conclusion: `Prop`, so `SimplyConnectedSpace X` is a property of the space, not extra data.

Its one field, `equiv_unit : Nonempty (FundamentalGroupoid X ≌ Discrete Unit)`, says that there is an equivalence of categories between the fundamental groupoid of $X$ and `Discrete Unit`, the category with a single object and a single morphism. The objects of the fundamental groupoid are the points of $X$, and its morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are the homotopy classes, relative to the endpoints, of paths from $x$ to $y$.

Such an equivalence exists exactly when $X$ is nonempty, any two points are joined by a path, and any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic relative to them. So this is the usual notion, a path-connected space with trivial fundamental group, in the form of its characterization by unique homotopy classes of paths.

- `≌` denotes an equivalence of categories, not an isomorphism: the fundamental groupoid may have many objects, all isomorphic, with exactly one morphism between any two.

## What it says
Every simply connected space is path-connected.

This is part of the usual notion of simple connectivity, under which a simply connected space is path-connected by definition. Here it follows from the groupoid definition, and Lean applies it by itself wherever $X$ is known to be simply connected.

## What it says
In a simply connected space, the fundamental group at every base point is trivial.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on a type $X$.
- `[SimplyConnectedSpace X]`: $X$ is simply connected: nonempty, with any two points joined by a path and any two paths with the same endpoints homotopic relative to them.
- `(x : X)`: a base point $x$ of $X$.
- The conclusion: `Subsingleton (FundamentalGroup X x)`, that is, any two elements of the fundamental group $\pi_1(X, x)$, the group of homotopy classes of loops at $x$, are equal.

A group always contains its identity, the class of the constant loop, so having at most one element means being the trivial group: $\pi_1(X, x) = 1$ for every $x$. This is the second half of the usual definition of a simply connected space, a path-connected space with trivial fundamental group.

## What it says
In a simply connected space, between any two points there is at most one homotopy class of paths.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on a type $X$.
- `[SimplyConnectedSpace X]`: $X$ is simply connected: its fundamental groupoid is equivalent to the category with one object and one morphism.
- `(x y : X)`: two points $x$ and $y$ of $X$, possibly equal.
- The conclusion: `Subsingleton (Path.Homotopic.Quotient x y)`, that is, any two elements of the set of paths from $x$ to $y$ taken up to homotopy relative to the endpoints are equal. Equivalently, any two paths from $x$ to $y$ are homotopic relative to their endpoints.

This is the uniqueness half of the characterization of simply connected spaces by a unique homotopy class of paths between any two points; the existence half is path-connectedness, which a separate instance provides. For $x = y$ it says that every loop at $x$ is null-homotopic.

## What it says
Every contractible space is simply connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y]`: a topology on the type `Y`.
- `[ContractibleSpace Y]`: $Y$ is contractible: it is homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
- The conclusion: `SimplyConnectedSpace Y`, that is, $Y$ is nonempty, any two of its points are joined by a path, and any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic relative to them.

This is the standard fact that a contractible space is path-connected with trivial fundamental group, stated for every topological space, with no local condition and no manifold or cell structure assumed.

## What it says
In a simply connected space, any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic relative to those endpoints.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on a type $X$.
- `[SimplyConnectedSpace X]`: $X$ is simply connected: its fundamental groupoid is equivalent to the category with one object and one morphism, so $X$ is nonempty and any two of its points are joined by a path.
- `(p₁ p₂ : Path x y)`: two paths $p_1, p_2$ from a point $x$ to a point $y$ of $X$, that is, continuous maps $[0,1] \to X$ sending $0$ to $x$ and $1$ to $y$; the endpoints $x$ and $y$ are implicit.
- The conclusion: `p₁.Homotopic p₂`, that is, there is a homotopy from $p_1$ to $p_2$ through paths from $x$ to $y$, keeping the endpoints fixed.

This is the uniqueness part of the characterization of simply connected spaces by unique homotopy classes of paths between any two points, stated for the paths themselves rather than for their classes.

## What it says
A topological space $X$ is strongly locally contractible when every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods that are contractible in their own right.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type `X`.
- The conclusion: `Prop`, so `StronglyLocallyContractibleSpace X` is a property of the space, not extra data.

Its one field, `contractible_basis`, says that for every point $x$ the neighborhood filter `𝓝 x` has as a basis the neighborhoods $s$ of $x$ that are contractible as subspaces: every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ which, with the topology induced from $X$, is homotopy equivalent to a point.

As the docstring says, this is stronger than the classical notion of local contractibility, which asks only that $V$ can be chosen with its inclusion into $U$ null-homotopic: here $V$ itself must be contractible. The word "strongly" in the name tells the two notions apart.

- "Has a basis" means that every set in `𝓝 x` contains one of the basis sets, which are themselves neighborhoods of $x$.
- `ContractibleSpace s` is about $s$ with the subspace topology, made a space of its own; contractibility includes nonemptiness, which holds anyway since $x \in s$.
- The empty space satisfies the condition, which says nothing when there are no points.

## What it says
Every strongly locally contractible space is locally contractible in the classical sense.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on a type $X$.
- `[StronglyLocallyContractibleSpace X]`: every point $x$ of $X$ has arbitrarily small neighborhoods that are contractible as subspaces: each neighborhood of $x$ contains a contractible one.
- The conclusion: `LocallyContractibleSpace X`, the classical notion that the docstring describes by null-homotopic inclusions: for every point $x$ and every neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there is a neighborhood $V \subseteq U$ of $x$ whose inclusion into $U$ is null-homotopic.

This is the easy implication between the two notions: a contractible neighborhood $V$ inside $U$ has a null-homotopic identity map, hence a null-homotopic inclusion into $U$. As the docstring says, the converse fails.

## What it says
A space in which every point has a neighborhood basis of sets contractible as subspaces is strongly locally contractible.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on a type $X$.
- `(h : ∀ (x : X), (nhds x).HasBasis (p x) (s x))`: for every point $x$, the sets $s(x, i)$, for the indices $i$ in a type $\iota$ with $p(x, i)$ true, form a basis of the neighborhoods of $x$: each is a neighborhood of $x$, and every neighborhood of $x$ contains one of them. Here $p$ and $s$ are implicit families, $p(x, i)$ a condition and $s(x, i)$ a subset of $X$.
- `(h' : ∀ (x : X) (i : ι), p x i → ContractibleSpace ↑(s x i))`: each selected set $s(x, i)$, one with $p(x, i)$ true, is contractible with the subspace topology.
- The conclusion: `StronglyLocallyContractibleSpace X`, that is, at every point the neighborhoods contractible as subspaces form a neighborhood basis.

This is the definition of strong local contractibility restated for a basis given in advance: any basis of contractible neighborhoods will do, not only the basis of all of them that the definition names.

## What it says
For a type `R` of scalars acting on a type `M` by a scalar multiplication $c \bullet x$, a `SubMulAction R M` is a subset of $M$ closed under multiplication by every scalar.

- `[SMul R M]`: a scalar multiplication $R \times M \to M$, $(c, x) \mapsto c \bullet x$, with no axiom required of it.
- The conclusion: `Type v`, so `SubMulAction R M` is the type of all such subsets of $M$, each carried with its proof of closure.

Its fields:

- `carrier : Set M`: the underlying subset $N \subseteq M$.
- `smul_mem'`: for every scalar $c \in R$ and every $x \in N$, $c \bullet x \in N$.

When $R$ is a group acting on $M$, this is a subset stable under the action, that is, a union of orbits. In general it asks only for closure under the given operation, with no associativity or identity law, and unlike a submodule it needs no addition and no zero.

## What it says
A `SubNegMonoid` structure on a type `G` is an additive monoid structure on `G` together with a negation $a \mapsto -a$, a subtraction $(a, b) \mapsto a - b$ and integer multiples $n \bullet a$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, such that subtracting is adding the negative and integer multiples are iterated sums.

- `(G : Type u_2)`: the type $G$ that carries the structure.

Its fields:

- from `AddMonoid G`: an associative addition $+$ on `G` with a neutral element $0$, and natural-number multiples;
- from `Neg G`, `Sub G` and `ZSMul G`: the operations $-a$, $a - b$ and $n \bullet a$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$;
- `sub`: the subtraction, by default $a - b := a + (-b)$;
- `sub_eq_add_neg`: $a - b = a + (-b)$ for all $a, b$ in `G`;
- `zsmul_zero'`, `zsmul_succ'`, `zsmul_neg'`: $0 \bullet a = 0$, $(n+1) \bullet a = n \bullet a + a$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $(-(n+1)) \bullet a = -((n+1) \bullet a)$.

So $n \bullet a$ is the $n$-fold sum $a + \dots + a$ for $n \ge 0$, and the negation of the $|n|$-fold sum for $n < 0$: subtraction and integer multiples are fixed by $+$ and $-$, and are fields only so that an instance can choose them with good definitional behaviour, as the docstring explains. Nothing says that $-a$ is an inverse of $a$. This is Mathlib's step between additive monoids and additive groups: an additive group is a `SubNegMonoid` in which also $-a + a = 0$.

## What it says
A subgroup of a group $G$: a subset of $G$ that contains $1$ and is closed under multiplication and under inverses.

- `(G : Type u_3)`: the type $G$ whose subgroups these are.
- `[Group G]`: a group structure on $G$, written multiplicatively, with identity $1$ and inverses $x^{-1}$.

Its fields:

- from `Submonoid G`: a subset of $G$, its `carrier`, that contains $1$ and with any $a$ and $b$ contains their product $ab$;
- `inv_mem'`: with any $x$ the carrier contains $x^{-1}$.

This is the standard definition: a subset $H$ of $G$ with $1 \in H$, and $ab \in H$ and $a^{-1} \in H$ for all $a, b \in H$. It is equivalent to asking that $H$ be a group under the operation of $G$ restricted to it, which is how many books first define a subgroup. No finiteness or commutativity is asked of $G$.

## What it says

The statement has no docstring of its own: it is the lemma that the definition `Subgroup.pathComponentOne` generates for its underlying set. It says that this subgroup is what its name promises, the path component of the identity, which in a topological group is a subgroup because products and inverses of paths starting at $1$ are again such paths. No more is asked of $G$ than being a topological group.

## What it says
For a topological group $G$, the path component of the identity $1$, as a subgroup of $G$.

- `(G : Type u_4)`: the type $G$ underlying the group.
- `[Group G] [TopologicalSpace G] [IsTopologicalGroup G]`: $G$ is a topological group, a group with a topology for which multiplication and inversion are continuous.
- The result is a `Subgroup G`, a subgroup of $G$.

Its value: as a submonoid, it is `.pathComponentOne G`, the path component of $1$ made a submonoid, so its underlying set is the set of the $g \in G$ that a continuous path in $G$ joins to $1$. The one field left, closure under inverses, holds because a path $\gamma$ from $1$ to $g$ gives the path $t \mapsto \gamma(t)^{-1}$ from $1$ to $g^{-1}$, inversion being continuous.

In a topological group the path component of the identity is a subgroup, indeed a normal one, and this is that standard object. Nothing more is asked of $G$: no connectedness, no separation axiom.

## What it says
If $g : Y \to Z$ induces the topology of $Y$, a map $f : X \to Y$ is continuous at a point $x$ exactly when $g \circ f$ is continuous at $x$.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Z]`: $Y$, $X$ and $Z$ are topological spaces.
- `(hg : IsInducing g)`: the map $g : Y \to Z$ induces the topology of $Y$: the open sets of $Y$ are exactly the preimages $g^{-1}(W)$ of the open sets $W$ of $Z$. The map need not be injective.
- The conclusion, `ContinuousAt f x ↔ ContinuousAt (g ∘ f) x`: for any map $f : X \to Y$ and any point $x \in X$, $f$ is continuous at $x$ (for each neighbourhood $U$ of $f(x)$, the preimage $f^{-1}(U)$ is a neighbourhood of $x$) exactly when $x \mapsto g(f(x))$ is continuous at $x$.

This is the pointwise form of the standard criterion for continuity into a subspace. In the induced topology, the neighbourhoods of $f(x)$ are the sets containing $g^{-1}(W)$ for a neighbourhood $W$ of $g(f(x))$, so testing $f$ against the neighbourhoods of $f(x)$ is testing $g \circ f$ against those of $g(f(x))$. Nothing is asked of $f$, and $g$ need not be injective, surjective or open.

## What it says

- `(h : Set.range f ∈ nhds (f x))`: for the point $x$ of $X$, the image $f(X)$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$ in $Y$, that is, it contains an open set containing $f(x)$.
- The conclusion, `ContinuousAt (g ∘ f) x ↔ ContinuousAt g (f x)`: $g \circ f$ is continuous at $x$ exactly when $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$.

This is the local character of continuity: when $f(X)$, with the topology it inherits, is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$, continuity of $g$ at $f(x)$ can be tested on it. The direction from $g$ to $g \circ f$ holds for every continuous $f$; the neighbourhood hypothesis gives the other, and cannot be dropped: for the inclusion of the one-point space $\{0\}$ into $\mathbb{R}$ and $g$ the indicator function of $\{0\}$, the composite is continuous and $g$ is not continuous at $0$.

The induced topology is the coarsest topology on $X$ making $f$ continuous, and a map is inducing when the topology of its domain is this one, so the statement holds by construction. ## What it says
The preimage of a compact set under an inducing map is compact, provided the set lies in the image of the map.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces, and $f : X \to Y$ is a function between them.
- `(hf : IsInducing f)`: $f$ is inducing: the topology of $X$ is the one pulled back from $Y$ along $f$, so the open sets of $X$ are exactly the preimages $f^{-1}(V)$ of the open sets $V$ of $Y$.
- `(hK : IsCompact K)`: $K$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
- `(Kf : K ⊆ Set.range f)`: $K$ is contained in the image $f(X)$.
- The conclusion, `IsCompact (f ⁻¹' K)`: the preimage $f^{-1}(K)$ is a compact subset of $X$.

An open cover of $f^{-1}(K)$ consists of sets $f^{-1}(V_i)$ with $V_i$ open in $Y$; because every point of $K$ is a value of $f$, the $V_i$ cover $K$, and a finite subcover of $K$ gives one of $f^{-1}(K)$. For a subspace inclusion it says that a compact subset of $Y$ lying in the subspace is compact in the subspace topology. The hypothesis `Kf` cannot be dropped: for the inclusion of $(0,1)$ into $\mathbb{R}$, the compact set $[0,1]$ has preimage $(0,1)$, which is not compact. No injectivity is needed.

## What it says
For an inducing map $f : X \to Y$, a subset $F$ of $X$ is path-connected if and only if its image $f(F)$ is path-connected; the docstring says the same, in the other order.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces, and $f : X \to Y$ is a function between them.
- `(hf : IsInducing f)`: $f$ is inducing: the topology of $X$ is the one pulled back from $Y$ along $f$, so the open sets of $X$ are exactly the preimages $f^{-1}(V)$ of the open sets $V$ of $Y$.
- The conclusion, `IsPathConnected F ↔ IsPathConnected (f '' F)`: for a subset $F \subseteq X$, $F$ is non-empty and any two of its points are joined by a path in $F$, exactly when the same holds for $f(F)$ in $Y$.

One direction is the general fact that a continuous image of a path-connected set is path-connected; an inducing map is continuous. For the other, a path $\gamma$ in $f(F)$ from $f(a)$ to $f(b)$ lifts to a map $\delta$ from $[0,1]$ into $F$ with $f \circ \delta = \gamma$, $\delta(0) = a$ and $\delta(1) = b$, by choosing a preimage in $F$ of each point; since $X$ carries the induced topology, $\delta$ is continuous because $f \circ \delta$ is. So no injectivity is needed; for an embedding this is the familiar invariance of path-connectedness under a homeomorphism onto the image.

## What it says
For an inducing map $f : \alpha \to \beta$, the image $f(s)$ of a subset $s$ of $\alpha$ is preconnected if and only if $s$ is.

- `[TopologicalSpace α] [TopologicalSpace β]`: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are topological spaces, and $f : \alpha \to \beta$ is a function between them.
- `(hf : IsInducing f)`: $f$ is inducing: the topology of $\alpha$ is the one pulled back from $\beta$ along $f$, so the open sets of $\alpha$ are exactly the preimages $f^{-1}(V)$ of the open sets $V$ of $\beta$.
- The conclusion, `IsPreconnected (f '' s) ↔ IsPreconnected s`: for a subset $s \subseteq \alpha$, $f(s)$ admits no separation by two open sets of $\beta$ exactly when $s$ admits none by two open sets of $\alpha$.

Preconnected means connected or empty: whenever two open sets cover the set and each meets it, they meet each other inside it. Continuity of $f$ gives the direction from $s$ to $f(s)$. Conversely, open sets $U = f^{-1}(U')$ and $V = f^{-1}(V')$ that separate $s$ come from open sets $U'$, $V'$ of $\beta$ that separate $f(s)$, since a point of $f(s) \cap U' \cap V'$ is $f(x)$ with $x \in s \cap U \cap V$. No injectivity is needed.

## What it says
If $g : Y \to Z$ is inducing, then for any map $f : X \to Y$, the composite $g \circ f$ is inducing if and only if $f$ is.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Z]`: $Y$, $X$ and $Z$ are topological spaces; $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$ are functions, not assumed continuous.
- `(hg : IsInducing g)`: $g$ is inducing: the topology of $Y$ is the one pulled back from $Z$ along $g$, so the open sets of $Y$ are exactly the preimages $g^{-1}(W)$ of the open sets $W$ of $Z$.
- The conclusion, `IsInducing (g ∘ f) ↔ IsInducing f`: the topology of $X$ is the one pulled back from $Z$ along $g \circ f$ exactly when it is the one pulled back from $Y$ along $f$.

Pulling a topology back in two steps is pulling it back along the composite: the preimages under $f$ of the open sets $g^{-1}(W)$ of $Y$ are the sets $(g \circ f)^{-1}(W)$. So the topology induced on $X$ by $g \circ f$ from $Z$ equals the one induced by $f$ from $Y$, and each side says that $X$ carries it; this is the transitivity of initial topologies. The direction from $f$ to $g \circ f$ is the familiar fact that a composite of inducing maps is inducing; the other lets one check that $f$ is inducing after composing with $g$. Neither map need be injective, and $f$ need not be assumed continuous: an inducing map is continuous.

## What it says
Every map out of a space with at most one point is inducing.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $Y$ and $X$ are topological spaces.
- `[Subsingleton X]`: $X$ has at most one element: it is empty or a single point.
- `(f : X → Y)`: an arbitrary function from $X$ to $Y$.

A set with at most one element carries exactly one topology: its only subsets are $\emptyset$ and the whole set, and both are open in every topology. So the given topology of $X$ and the one induced by $f$ coincide, whatever $Y$ and $f$ are. No condition on $Y$ and no continuity of $f$ is assumed; $f$ is continuous anyway, as every map out of such a space is.

## What it says
The composite of two open embeddings is an open embedding.

- The conclusion, `IsOpenEmbedding (g ∘ f)`: the composite $x \mapsto g(f(x))$ is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto an open subspace of $Z$.

Injectivity and the induced topology pass to composites, and the image $g(f(X))$ is open in $Z$ because $f(X)$ is open in $Y$ and an open embedding maps open sets to open sets. This is the standard fact that an open subset of an open subspace is open in the whole space, transported along the two maps. No separation or non-emptiness condition is assumed.

- `IsOrderedMonoid` is a property added on top of the monoid and the preorder, both carried as typeclasses (in square brackets): Lean finds all three by itself.
- The attribute `@[to_additive]` makes from the same text the additive version: the additive units of an ordered additive commutative monoid form an ordered additive commutative group.
- `Type u_1` says that $\alpha$ is a type, Lean's version of a set; the universe level does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
For a group with zero $G_0$ and a nonzero element $a$ of it, `Units.mk0 a ha` is $a$ seen as an element of the unit group $G_0^\times$, with inverse $a^{-1}$.

- `[GroupWithZero G₀]`: $G_0$, a type in the universe `u_3`, is a group with zero: a monoid with an absorbing zero, in which $0 \neq 1$ and every nonzero element has a two-sided inverse $a^{-1}$. Fields and division rings are examples.
- `(a : G₀)`: an element $a$ of $G_0$.
- `(ha : a ≠ 0)`: a proof that $a \neq 0$.
- The result has type `G₀ˣ`, the group of units of $G_0$: its elements are the invertible elements of $G_0$, each recorded together with its inverse and the two equations that make it one.

Its value is `⟨a, a⁻¹, mul_inv_cancel₀ ha, inv_mul_cancel₀ ha⟩`: the unit whose underlying element is $a$ and whose inverse is $a^{-1}$, with the equations $a a^{-1} = 1$ and $a^{-1} a = 1$, which hold because $a \neq 0$.

This is the standard fact that in a group with zero, as in a field, every nonzero element is a unit; `Units.mk0` is the map from nonzero elements to units that it gives. As the docstring says, together with the division `/ₚ` by a unit it lets one write $a / b$ as a function of three arguments: $a$, $b$ and a proof that $b \neq 0$.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- `G₀ˣ` is Lean's `Units G₀`. A unit is a package, not a bare element: an element, an inverse and proofs of the two equations. The coercion `↑(Units.mk0 a ha)` gives back $a$, and two units with the same underlying element are equal, since inverses in a monoid are unique.
- In a group with zero the inverse is a total function, with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$. The hypothesis `ha` keeps $a$ away from $0$, so that value plays no part here.
- `ha` is a proof, and Lean treats any two proofs of `a ≠ 0` as equal, so the unit depends on $a$ alone.
- `[GroupWithZero G₀]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass: Lean finds the structure by itself. It includes $0 \neq 1$, so $0$ is never a unit, and the hypothesis `ha` is exactly the condition for $a$ to be one.
- `Type u_3` says that $G_0$ is a type, Lean's version of a set; `u_3` is its universe level, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
In a monoid, a unit times its inverse is $1$: for every unit $a$ of a monoid $\alpha$, $a \cdot a^{-1} = 1$, computed in $\alpha$.

- `[Monoid α]`: $\alpha$, a type in the universe `u`, is a monoid: it has an associative multiplication with an identity $1$. Nothing more is assumed; in particular $\alpha$ has no inverse operation of its own.
- `(a : αˣ)`: a unit $a$ of $\alpha$, an element of the group of units `αˣ`: an invertible element of $\alpha$ recorded together with its two-sided inverse.
- The conclusion: `↑a * ↑a⁻¹ = 1`. Here `↑a` is the element of $\alpha$ underlying the unit $a$, `a⁻¹` is the inverse of $a$ in the group of units, and `↑a⁻¹` is the element of $\alpha$ underlying that inverse. Their product in $\alpha$, with $a$ on the left, is the identity.

This is the defining property of an inverse, on the right: a unit's inverse is a right inverse of it. The statement holds for every monoid, the setting in which units are defined, so it is in the generality of the notion.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- `αˣ` is Lean's `Units α`. A unit is a package, not a bare element: an element, an inverse and proofs that their products in both orders are $1$. The arrow `↑` is the coercion that forgets the package and keeps the element. The equation here is the stored right-inverse law; the product in the other order is the subject of a separate statement.
- `↑a⁻¹` is read as `↑(a⁻¹)`: the inverse is taken in the group of units, which is the only place an inverse exists, and then turned back into an element of $\alpha$.
- `[Monoid α]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass: Lean finds the monoid structure by itself.
- The attribute `@[to_additive (attr := simp)]` also makes the additive version, for additive units of an additive monoid, $a + (-a) = 0$, and marks both as rewriting rules that Lean's simplifier uses on its own.
- In the trivial monoid, with one element, both sides are that element, so there is no exceptional case.

## What it says
Two units of a preordered monoid compare as units exactly when their underlying elements compare: for units $a, b$ of $\alpha$, $a \le b$ in the group of units if and only if $a \le b$ in $\alpha$.

- `[Monoid α]`: $\alpha$, a type in the universe `u_1`, is a monoid, an associative multiplication with an identity $1$, so that it has a group of units `αˣ`: the invertible elements, each recorded with its inverse.
- `[Preorder α]`: $\alpha$ also carries a preorder $\le$, a reflexive and transitive relation. No link between the order and the multiplication is assumed: $\alpha$ need not be an ordered monoid.
- The units $a, b$ of $\alpha$ are implicit arguments, which Lean reads off from the statement.
- The conclusion: `↑a ≤ ↑b ↔ a ≤ b`. On the left, `↑a` and `↑b` are the elements of $\alpha$ underlying the units, compared in $\alpha$; on the right, the units themselves are compared by the preorder that Lean puts on `αˣ`.

So the preorder on the group of units is the one it inherits from $\alpha$ through the inclusion of units into $\alpha$: the standard way to order a subset of an ordered set. The statement is as general as the notion, since it asks only for a monoid and a preorder on the same type.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- `αˣ` is Lean's `Units α`, and `↑` is the coercion that sends a unit to its underlying element of $\alpha$. This map is injective, since the inverse of an element is unique, so the inherited relation is again a preorder, and a partial order when that of $\alpha$ is one.
- `[Monoid α]` and `[Preorder α]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. They are separate: nothing says that multiplying by a unit preserves $\le$, and the statement does not need it.
- The attribute `@[to_additive (attr := simp, norm_cast)]` also makes the additive version, for the additive units of an additive monoid, and marks both as rules for Lean's simplifier and for its tactic that moves coercions, which use them on their own.

## What it says
Two units of a preordered monoid compare strictly as units exactly when their underlying elements do: for units $a, b$ of $\alpha$, $a < b$ in the group of units if and only if $a < b$ in $\alpha$.

- `[Monoid α]`: $\alpha$, a type in the universe `u_1`, is a monoid, an associative multiplication with an identity $1$, so that it has a group of units `αˣ`: the invertible elements, each recorded with its inverse.
- `[Preorder α]`: $\alpha$ also carries a preorder $\le$, a reflexive and transitive relation, with its strict relation: $x < y$ when $x \le y$ and not $y \le x$. No link between the order and the multiplication is assumed.
- The units $a, b$ of $\alpha$ are implicit arguments, which Lean reads off from the statement.
- The conclusion: `↑a < ↑b ↔ a < b`. On the left, `↑a` and `↑b` are the elements of $\alpha$ underlying the units, compared strictly in $\alpha$; on the right, the units themselves are compared by the strict relation of the preorder that Lean puts on `αˣ`.

So the strict order on the group of units, like the order itself, is the one inherited from $\alpha$ through the inclusion of units into $\alpha$, as for any subset of a preordered set. The preorder of $\alpha$ need not be linear, and the order on units is not reversed or changed by taking inverses.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- `αˣ` is Lean's `Units α`, and `↑` is the coercion that sends a unit to its underlying element of $\alpha$, an injective map.
- In a preorder, Lean's `<` is the strict relation of `≤`: $x < y$ means $x \le y$ and not $y \le x$. When $\le$ is only a preorder this is stronger than $x \le y$ and $x \neq y$, on units as on $\alpha$, and the statement holds for it in this sense.
- `[Monoid α]` and `[Preorder α]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. They are separate: nothing says that multiplying by a unit preserves $<$, and the statement does not need it.
- The attribute `@[to_additive (attr := simp, norm_cast)]` also makes the additive version, for the additive units of an additive monoid, and marks both as rules for Lean's simplifier and for its tactic that moves coercions, which use them on their own.

## What it says
Integer powers of a unit can be taken in the group of units or in the ambient monoid, with the same result: for a unit $u$ of a division monoid $\alpha$ and an integer $n$, the element of $\alpha$ underlying $u^n$ is $u^n$ computed in $\alpha$.

- `[DivisionMonoid α]`: $\alpha$, a type in the universe `u_1`, is a division monoid: a monoid with an inverse operation $x \mapsto x^{-1}$ defined on all of $\alpha$, with $(x^{-1})^{-1} = x$ and $(xy)^{-1} = y^{-1}x^{-1}$, and with $x^{-1} = y$ whenever $xy = 1$. Groups, and groups with zero such as fields, are examples. It gives $\alpha$ integer powers, with $x^{-m} = (x^m)^{-1}$ for $m > 0$.
- `(u : αˣ)`: a unit $u$ of $\alpha$, an element of the group of units `αˣ`: an invertible element recorded with its inverse.
- `(n : ℤ)`: an integer $n$, which may be negative.
- The conclusion: `↑(u ^ n) = ↑u ^ n`. On the left, $u^n$ is taken in the group `αˣ` and then mapped to $\alpha$ by `↑`; on the right, the element `↑u` of $\alpha$ is raised to the power $n$ in $\alpha$.

For $n \ge 0$ this is the multiplicativity of the inclusion of units into $\alpha$. For $n < 0$ the right side uses the inverse operation of $\alpha$, and the statement says that on a unit it is the unit's inverse. Not every element of $\alpha$ need be a unit, so the statement is about the units alone, as it should be.

## References and tests
No reference is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- The two powers use two inverses: the left side the inverse that a unit carries, the right side the inverse operation of $\alpha$, which is total. In a group with zero it has the value $0^{-1} = 0$ at the element $0$, which is not a unit (unless $\alpha$ is trivial), so that value never enters here.
- `ℤ` exponents are Lean's integer powers; for $n \ge 0$ they are the ordinary powers, and $n = 0$ gives $1$ on both sides.
- `αˣ` is Lean's `Units α`, and `↑` is the coercion that sends a unit to its underlying element of $\alpha$.
- `[DivisionMonoid α]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass: Lean finds the structure by itself.
- The attribute `@[to_additive (attr := simp, norm_cast)]` also makes the additive version, for integer multiples of additive units of an additive division monoid, and marks both as rules for Lean's simplifier and for its tactic that moves coercions.

## What it says
The cusp function of $f$ for the period $h$: the function $F$ of $q$ with $f(\tau) = F(e^{2\pi i \tau/h})$, extended to $q = 0$ by its limit there.

- `(h : ℝ)`: a real number $h$, the period, or width of the cusp at $i\infty$.
- `(f : UpperHalfPlane → ℂ)`: a complex-valued function $f$ on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H} = \{\tau \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}\tau > 0\}$.
- The result is a function $F : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$.

Its value is `Function.Periodic.cuspFunction h (f ∘ ofComplex)`. First $f$ is extended to all of $\mathbb{C}$ by `ofComplex`, which sends a point of $\mathbb{H}$ to itself and every other complex number to one unspecified point of $\mathbb{H}$. Then $F(q)$, for $q \neq 0$, is the value at $\tau = \frac{h}{2\pi i}\log q$, a point with $e^{2\pi i\tau/h} = q$; and $F(0)$ is the limit of $F(q)$ as $q \to 0$, $q \neq 0$.

This is the standard passage from a periodic function on $\mathbb{H}$ to a function of $q$: for $h > 0$, $\tau \mapsto e^{2\pi i\tau/h}$ maps $\mathbb{H}$ onto the punctured disk $0 < |q| < 1$, and a function of period $h$ factors through it. When $f$ is moreover holomorphic and bounded as $\operatorname{Im}\tau \to \infty$, $F$ is holomorphic at $0$ as well, and its Taylor coefficients are the $q$-expansion coefficients of $f$.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl [`cmf.fouriercoefficients`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/cmf/cmf.fouriercoefficients) — the Fourier coefficients of a classical modular form, the Taylor coefficients of its cusp function.
- `UpperHalfPlane.eq_cuspFunction` — for $h \neq 0$ and $f$ of period $h$, $F(e^{2\pi i\tau/h}) = f(\tau)$ for every $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$: the property the docstring names.
- `UpperHalfPlane.cuspFunction_apply_zero` — for $h > 0$ and $f$ of period $h$, when $F$ is analytic at $0$, $F(0)$ is the value of $f$ at $i\infty$, the limit of $f(\tau)$ as $\operatorname{Im}\tau \to \infty$.

The first test shows that away from $0$ the function is the one meant; the second, that the value chosen at $0$ is the expected one whenever $F$ is analytic there.

## Lean subtleties
- The definition is total: it takes any real $h$ and any $f$, periodic or not, and has a value at every $q$. The values mean what the docstring says only for $h > 0$, $f$ of period $h$ and $|q| < 1$. For $h = 0$, Lean's convention $x / 0 = 0$ gives $\tau = 0$ for every $q$, so $F$ is constant off $0$, with an unspecified value.
- At $q = 0$ the value is chosen by Lean's `limUnder`: the limit when there is one, which is then unique, and an unspecified complex number otherwise. This is the docstring's "choice of limit".
- `ofComplex` only makes $f$ a function on all of $\mathbb{C}$: for $h > 0$ and $0 < |q| < 1$ the point $\tau$ has $\operatorname{Im}\tau > 0$, so only genuine values of $f$ enter there.
- $\log$ is the principal branch. For $f$ of period $h$ the branch does not matter: two choices of $\tau$ differ by an integer multiple of $h$.

## What it says
A holomorphic function on the upper half-plane that has period $h > 0$ and is bounded at $i\infty$ is the sum of its $q$-expansion: $f(\tau) = \sum_{m \ge 0} a_m q^m$ with $q = e^{2\pi i\tau/h}$, at every $\tau$.

Here $h$ is a real number and $f$ a complex-valued function on $\mathbb{H} = \{\tau \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}\tau > 0\}$, both implicit.

- `(hh : 0 < h)`: the period $h$ is positive.
- `(hfper : Function.Periodic (f ∘ ↑ofComplex) ↑h)`: $f$ has period $h$, stated for $f$ extended to all of $\mathbb{C}$ by `ofComplex`; it amounts to $f(\tau + h) = f(\tau)$ for $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$.
- `(hfhol : MDiff f)`: $f$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{H}$.
- `(hfbdd : IsBoundedAtImInfty f)`: $f$ is bounded at $i\infty$: there are $A$ and $C$ with $|f(\tau)| \le C$ whenever $\operatorname{Im}\tau \ge A$.
- `(τ : UpperHalfPlane)`: a point $\tau$ of $\mathbb{H}$.
- The conclusion: the series whose $m$-th term is $a_m q^m$, where $a_m$ is the coefficient `PowerSeries.coeff m` of the formal power series `qExpansion h f` and $q$ = `Function.Periodic.qParam h ↑τ` $= e^{2\pi i\tau/h}$, has sum $f(\tau)$.

This is the classical $q$-expansion of a periodic holomorphic function, as for a modular form at the cusp $i\infty$: periodicity makes $f$ a function of $q$ on the punctured disk, boundedness removes the singularity at $q = 0$, and the Taylor series at $0$ converges to $f$ on all of $\mathbb{H}$, since $|q| = e^{-2\pi \operatorname{Im}\tau/h} < 1$. Only $m \ge 0$ appear, because of the boundedness.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl [`cmf.fouriercoefficients`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/cmf/cmf.fouriercoefficients) — the expansion $f(\tau) = \sum a_n q^n$ of a modular form, which this theorem proves for $h = 1$.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `HasSum` is unconditional convergence: the sums over finite sets of indices tend to $f(\tau)$. For a series of complex numbers this is the same as absolute convergence, stronger than convergence of the partial sums.
- `qExpansion h f` is defined for every $f$, as the formal power series of the Taylor coefficients at $0$ of the cusp function of $f$; this theorem is what ties it to $f$ under the four hypotheses.
- `MDiff f` is differentiability as a map of complex manifolds; for $\mathbb{H}$, an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$, it is holomorphy.
- `ofComplex` sends a point of $\mathbb{H}$ to itself and every other complex number to one fixed point of $\mathbb{H}$, so the extended function is constant off $\mathbb{H}$, and its periodicity is that of $f$.
- `↑τ` is $\tau$ as a complex number, and `•` is scalar multiplication, here the product of complex numbers.

## What it says
The integrand of the Petersson scalar product in weight $k$: at a point $\tau = x + iy$ of the upper half-plane, the complex number $\overline{f(\tau)}\, f'(\tau)\, y^k$.

- `(k : ℤ)`: an integer $k$, the weight.
- `(f f' : UpperHalfPlane → ℂ)`: two complex-valued functions $f, f'$ on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H} = \{\tau \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}\tau > 0\}$.
- `(τ : UpperHalfPlane)`: a point $\tau$ of $\mathbb{H}$.
- The result is a complex number.

Its value is `conj (f τ) * f' τ * τ.im ^ k`: the complex conjugate of $f(\tau)$, times $f'(\tau)$, times the $k$-th power of the imaginary part $y = \operatorname{Im}\tau$.

For two modular forms of weight $k$ for a group $\Gamma$, the factor $y^k$ makes this function invariant under $\Gamma$, and the Petersson scalar product integrates it over a fundamental domain against the invariant measure $dx\,dy/y^2$, which is not part of this function. Many texts conjugate the second form instead, $f(\tau)\overline{g(\tau)}y^k$; this definition conjugates the first, as Lean's inner products do, so it is conjugate-linear in $f$ and linear in $f'$. The two conventions differ by exchanging the functions, or by complex conjugation.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl [`cmf.petersson_scalar_product`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/cmf/cmf.petersson_scalar_product) — the Petersson scalar product, integrated over a fundamental domain and divided by the group index; its integrand conjugates the second form rather than the first.
- `UpperHalfPlane.petersson_symm` — exchanging $f$ and $f'$ conjugates the value: the conjugate symmetry of a Hermitian form, and the passage between the two conventions.
- `UpperHalfPlane.petersson_slash_SL` — for $g \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, slashing both functions by $g$ in weight $k$ gives the integrand at $g \cdot \tau$.

The second test is the invariance that matters: for weight-$k$ forms invariant under $g$, the integrand takes the same value at $\tau$ and at $g \cdot \tau$, so its integral over $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ makes sense.

## Lean subtleties
- `conj` is complex conjugation, which the tests write `starRingEnd ℂ`.
- `τ.im ^ k` is an integer power of a positive real number, so a negative weight is allowed and no junk value at $0$ can occur.
- $f$ and $f'$ are arbitrary functions: nothing asks them to be holomorphic or modular of weight $k$. The value is pointwise; no integral is formed and no convergence is claimed.
- `UpperHalfPlane`, written $\mathbb{H}$, is the type of complex numbers with positive imaginary part, and `τ.im` is the imaginary part of $\tau$.

## What it says
The $q$-expansion of a function $f$ on the upper half-plane for the period $h$: the formal power series $\sum_{m \ge 0} a_m q^m$ whose coefficients are the Taylor coefficients at $q = 0$ of the cusp function $F$ of $f$, where $q = e^{2\pi i\tau/h}$.

- `(h : ℝ)`: a real number $h$, the period, or width of the cusp at $i\infty$.
- `(f : UpperHalfPlane → ℂ)`: a complex-valued function $f$ on $\mathbb{H} = \{\tau \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}\tau > 0\}$.
- The result is a formal power series with complex coefficients.

Its value is `.mk fun m ↦ (↑m.factorial)⁻¹ * iteratedDeriv m (cuspFunction h f) 0`: the series whose $m$-th coefficient is $a_m = F^{(m)}(0)/m!$, with $F$ = `cuspFunction h f`, the function of $q$ with $f(\tau) = F(e^{2\pi i\tau/h})$, extended to $q = 0$ by its limit there.

This is the standard $q$-expansion $f(\tau) = \sum a_n q^n$ of a periodic holomorphic function bounded at $i\infty$, such as a modular form at the cusp $i\infty$. For $h = 1$ it is the usual expansion in $q = e^{2\pi i\tau}$; a wider cusp takes its own period. The factor $1/m!$ is the Taylor normalisation, under which the $a_m$ are the Fourier coefficients of $f$.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl [`cmf.fouriercoefficients`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/cmf/cmf.fouriercoefficients) — the Fourier coefficients $a_n$ in the expansion $f(\tau) = \sum a_n q^n$.
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl [`cmf.q-expansion`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/cmf/cmf.q-expansion) — the $q$-expansion of a modular form.
- `UpperHalfPlane.hasSum_qExpansion` — for $h > 0$ and $f$ holomorphic, of period $h$ and bounded at $i\infty$, the series $\sum_m a_m q^m$ converges to $f(\tau)$ at every $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$.
- `ModularForm.qExpansion_injective` — for $h > 0$ a strict period of a subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, two modular forms of the same weight for $\Gamma$ with the same $q$-expansion are equal.

The two tests show that the series is the $q$-expansion in the analytic sense: it sums back to $f$, and it determines a modular form.

## Lean subtleties
- The definition is total: it takes any real $h$ and any $f$. The $a_m$ are Taylor coefficients of an analytic function only when $F$ is analytic at $0$, as under the hypotheses of the first test. Otherwise they can be junk: Lean's derivative of a function that is not differentiable at a point is $0$ there.
- `iteratedDeriv m F 0` is the $m$-th derivative of $F$ at $0$, and `(↑m.factorial)⁻¹` is $1/m!$ as a complex number.
- The constant term is $a_0 = F(0)$, the limit chosen by `cuspFunction` at $0$: the limit of $f$ at $i\infty$ when there is one.
- `PowerSeries ℂ` is the ring of formal power series: no convergence is part of the definition. A strict period of $\Gamma$ is an $h$ such that the translation $\tau \mapsto \tau + h$ lies in $\Gamma$.

## What it says
A weak extended metric space: a type `α` with a topology and a weak extended pseudometric structure in which distinct points are at nonzero distance.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: `α`, a type in the universe `u`, carries a topology, given in advance as a parameter of the class rather than defined by the distance.
- `extends WeakPseudoEMetricSpace α`: the class contains every field of a weak extended pseudometric space on `α`: an extended distance `edist x y`, with values in $[0, \infty]$, that vanishes on the diagonal, is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality, together with the condition of that class relating the distance to the given topology.

It adds one field:

- `eq_of_edist_eq_zero`: for all points $x, y$ of `α`, if $d(x, y) = 0$ then $x = y$.

With $d(x, x) = 0$ from the parent class, this is the docstring's condition $d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y$. It is the separation axiom that turns an extended pseudometric into an extended metric, exactly as an extended metric space adds it to an extended pseudometric space: two distinct points are at a positive distance, which may be $\infty$. The word "weak" concerns the link between the distance and the topology, which this class inherits unchanged.

## References and tests
No reference stating it in this form is recorded for it, and no test.

## Lean subtleties
- The distance takes values in `ℝ≥0∞`, the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$: points may be at infinite distance, and the separation axiom says nothing about such pairs beyond their being distinct.
- The topology is a parameter in square brackets: Lean finds it by itself, and the class does not make it the topology of the distance.
- Only the direction $d(x, y) = 0 \Rightarrow x = y$ is a field; the converse is the parent's axiom $d(x, x) = 0$.
- `extends` means that an instance of this class is an instance of the parent class with one more property, and Lean uses it as one.
- On the empty type and on a one-point type the new condition holds automatically.

## What it says
A weak extended pseudometric space: a type `α` with a given topology and an extended distance satisfying the axioms of an extended pseudometric, where the topology need not be the one the distance defines, but is coarser and agrees with it on each set of points at finite distance from one another.

- `[τ : TopologicalSpace α]`: `α`, a type in the universe `u`, carries a topology, named `τ`, given in advance.
- `extends EDist α`: the class contains an extended distance `edist x y`, written $d(x, y)$ here, with values in $[0, \infty]$.

Its fields, besides the distance:

- `edist_self`: $d(x, x) = 0$.
- `edist_comm`: $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$.
- `edist_triangle`: $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.
- `topology_le`: the topology of the distance, built from it by `uniformSpaceOfEDist`, is $\le$ `τ` in Lean's order on topologies: every `τ`-open set is open for the distance. So `τ` is coarser than the topology of the distance, or equal to it.

## What it says
A Weierstrass curve over a type `R`, a type in the universe `u`, is the data of five elements of `R`: the coefficients of the Weierstrass equation
$$Y^2 + a_1 XY + a_3 Y = X^3 + a_2 X^2 + a_4 X + a_6.$$

Its fields are the five coefficients, in this order:

- `a₁`, `a₂`, `a₃`, `a₄`, `a₆`: elements of `R`, the coefficients $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_6$ of the equation above.

No other field is present: no condition on the coefficients, and nothing about points.

This is the general, or long, Weierstrass equation with the standard indexing: $a_i$ has weight $i$, which is why there is no $a_5$, and the signs and the placement of the terms are the usual ones. As with a Weierstrass equation in the literature, the curve may be singular: $Y^2 = X^3$, with every coefficient $0$, is one. Being elliptic, or smooth, is a separate condition on the coefficients, and the equation, its points and their group law are built from this data separately.

As the docstring explains, the node is at $x_0 = (18b_6 - b_2b_4)/c_4$, and its tangent cone is $v^2 + a_1uv - (3x_0 + a_2)u^2$, with no vertical tangent; the slopes $T = v/u$ of the tangents are the roots of $T^2 + a_1T - (3x_0 + a_2)$, and multiplying by $c_4$, a unit at a node, gives the polynomial above. ## What it says
In a locally path-connected space $X$, the connected components and the path components form the same partition of $X$. So the set of connected components and the set of path components are in canonical bijection, and this definition is that bijection.

The value: the forward map sends the connected component of a point $x$ to the path component of the same $x$. It is well defined because, in a locally path-connected space, two points lie in the same connected component exactly when a path joins them (`connectedComponent_eq_iff_joined`). Both maps are induced by the identity of $X$, so each undoes the other.

This is the standard fact that in a locally path-connected space the path components are open, hence also closed, and so they coincide with the connected components. The equivalence is the canonical one, and it chooses no representatives.

## What it says
A topological space is contractible exactly when its identity map is homotopic to a constant map.

- `[TopologicalSpace Y]`: a topology on the type `Y`, an explicit argument `(Y : Type u_1)`.
- The conclusion: `ContractibleSpace Y`, that $Y$ is contractible, holds if and only if `(ContinuousMap.id Y).Nullhomotopic` holds. `ContractibleSpace Y` means that $Y$ is homotopy equivalent to a one-point space. `(ContinuousMap.id Y).Nullhomotopic` means that the identity map of $Y$, as a continuous map, is homotopic to the constant map at some point $y$ of $Y$.

This is the standard equivalence between the two usual definitions of contractibility, having the homotopy type of a point and having a nullhomotopic identity. Both sides need a point of $Y$: a homotopy equivalence with a point gives a map from the point into $Y$, and nullhomotopy names the constant value $y$. So the statement needs no separate nonemptiness hypothesis.

## What it says

It says that the neighbourhood filter of $x$ has as a basis the sets $s$ with three properties: $s$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, $s$ with the subspace topology is contractible, and $s \subseteq U$. Concretely, a set $t$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains such an $s$.

## What it says
In a real or complex inner product space, scaling the second vector by $r$ multiplies the inner product by $r$ itself, with no conjugation: $\langle x, r y\rangle = r \, \langle x, y\rangle$.

- `[RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$; `RCLike` is the class of fields that behave like one of them, with a conjugation, real and imaginary parts and an absolute value.
- `[SeminormedAddCommGroup E]`: $E$ is an abelian group with a seminorm $\|\cdot\|$, a norm that may vanish on nonzero vectors.
- `[InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E]`: $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{K}$ with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : E \times E \to \mathbb{K}$ that induces the given seminorm, $\|x\|^2 = \operatorname{Re}\langle x, x\rangle$.
- `(x y : E)`: two vectors $x$ and $y$ of $E$.
- `(r : 𝕜)`: a scalar $r \in \mathbb{K}$.
- The conclusion: `inner 𝕜 x (r • y) = r * inner 𝕜 x y`, the inner product of $x$ with $r y$ is $r$ times the inner product of $x$ with $y$.

This is homogeneity of the inner product in its second argument, in the convention Mathlib uses throughout: linear in the second argument and conjugate-linear in the first. Many texts take the other convention, linear in the first argument, where the same property reads $\langle r x, y\rangle = r \langle x, y\rangle$; over $\mathbb{R}$ the two conventions agree.

## Lean subtleties
- `[RCLike 𝕜]`, `[SeminormedAddCommGroup E]` and `[InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds the field, the seminorm and the inner product by itself.
- Convention: in Mathlib the second argument is the linear one, as in physics; the conjugate falls on the first (see `inner_smul_left`). With $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{C}$, scaling $y$ by $i$ multiplies the inner product by $i$.
- `r • y` is scalar multiplication, and `inner 𝕜 x y` is written `⟪x, y⟫` in the source.
- Since $E$ is only seminormed, the statement covers degenerate inner products too; the case $r = 0$ is included, where both sides are $0$.
- The docstring points to `inner_smul_right_eq_smul`, the version for scalars acting through a more general algebra.

## What it says
In a real or complex inner product space, the inner product of a vector with a finite sum, taken in the second argument, is the sum of the inner products: $\langle x, \sum_{i \in s} f_i\rangle = \sum_{i \in s} \langle x, f_i\rangle$.

- `[RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$; `RCLike` is the class of fields that behave like one of them, with a conjugation, real and imaginary parts and an absolute value.
- `[SeminormedAddCommGroup E]`: $E$ is an abelian group with a seminorm $\|\cdot\|$, a norm that may vanish on nonzero vectors.
- `[InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E]`: $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{K}$ with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : E \times E \to \mathbb{K}$ that induces the given seminorm, $\|x\|^2 = \operatorname{Re}\langle x, x\rangle$.
- `(s : Finset ι)`: a finite set $s$ of indices, taken from an index type $\iota$ that may itself be infinite.
- `(f : ι → E)`: a family $f$ of vectors $f_i \in E$, one for each index $i$.
- `(x : E)`: a vector $x$ of $E$.
- The conclusion: `inner 𝕜 x (∑ i ∈ s, f i) = ∑ i ∈ s, inner 𝕜 x (f i)`, the inner product of $x$ with the sum of the $f_i$ over $i \in s$ equals the sum over $i \in s$ of the inner products $\langle x, f_i\rangle$.

This is additivity of the inner product in its second argument, extended by induction from two terms to any finite sum; it holds with no convergence or completeness hypothesis, since only finitely many terms occur.

- A `Finset ι` is a finite subset of $\iota$; the sums `∑ i ∈ s, …` run over it only, so nothing about $\iota$ being finite is needed.

## What it says
For a real inner product space $F$, `innerₗ F` is its inner product seen as a bilinear map: the real-linear map sending $x \in F$ to the real-linear functional $y \mapsto \langle x, y\rangle$.

- `[SeminormedAddCommGroup F]`: $F$ is an abelian group with a seminorm $\|\cdot\|$, a norm that may vanish on nonzero vectors.
- `[InnerProductSpace ℝ F]`: $F$ is a real vector space with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : F \times F \to \mathbb{R}$, symmetric and bilinear, that induces the given seminorm, $\|x\|^2 = \langle x, x\rangle$.
- The type `F →ₗ[ℝ] F →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ`: real-linear maps from $F$ to the space of real-linear maps $F \to \mathbb{R}$, which is a bilinear form on $F$ written in curried form, one argument at a time.

Its value is `innerₛₗ ℝ`, the inner product packaged as a sesquilinear map (conjugate-linear in the first argument, linear in the second) for the field $\mathbb{R}$, where conjugation is the identity, so that sesquilinear means bilinear. Applied to $x$ and then to $y$ it gives $\langle x, y\rangle$.

Over $\mathbb{R}$ an inner product is by definition linear in each argument, so this is the standard picture of a real inner product as a symmetric bilinear form, positive semidefinite here since $F$ is only seminormed.

## What it says
For a real or complex inner product space $E$, `innerₛₗ 𝕜` is its inner product seen as a sesquilinear map: the map sending $v \in E$ to the linear functional $w \mapsto \langle v, w\rangle$, which is conjugate-linear in $v$ and linear in $w$.

- `(𝕜 : Type u_1)` with `[RCLike 𝕜]`: the scalar field `𝕜`, written $\mathbb{K}$ here, is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$; `RCLike` is the class of fields that behave like one of them, with a conjugation, real and imaginary parts and an absolute value.
- `[SeminormedAddCommGroup E]`: $E$ is an abelian group with a seminorm $\|\cdot\|$, a norm that may vanish on nonzero vectors.
- `[InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E]`: $E$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{K}$ with an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : E \times E \to \mathbb{K}$ that induces the given seminorm, $\|x\|^2 = \operatorname{Re}\langle x, x\rangle$.
- The type `E →ₗ⋆[𝕜] E →ₗ[𝕜] 𝕜`: conjugate-linear maps from $E$ to the space of $\mathbb{K}$-linear maps $E \to \mathbb{K}$, which is a sesquilinear form on $E$ written in curried form, one argument at a time.

Its value is $v \mapsto (w \mapsto \langle v, w\rangle)$, assembled by `LinearMap.mk₂'ₛₗ` from the inner product and the four facts that make it sesquilinear: additivity in each argument, $\langle a v, w\rangle = \bar a \langle v, w\rangle$ and $\langle v, a w\rangle = a \langle v, w\rangle$.

An inner product is a sesquilinear form, and this is it, with Mathlib's choice of which argument carries the conjugate. When $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ conjugation is the identity and the map is bilinear, as the docstring notes.

## What it says
The extended real numbers $[-\infty, +\infty]$ form a commutative additive monoid: their addition is associative and commutative, with $0$ as identity.

- The conclusion: `AddCommMonoid EReal`, a commutative monoid structure, written additively, on `EReal`, Mathlib's extended real line $\mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$.

The instance has no value of its own: it comes from the `deriving` clause of the definition of `EReal`, whose value is `WithBot (WithTop ℝ)`, the reals with a top element $+\infty$ adjoined and then a bottom element $-\infty$. The data is the structure of that type:

- zero is the real number $0$;
- two reals add as reals;
- $+\infty + x = +\infty$ for every $x$ other than $-\infty$;
- $-\infty + x = -\infty$ for every $x$, $+\infty$ included.

On the sums classical arithmetic defines, this is the usual addition of extended reals. It is extended to all pairs by setting $(-\infty) + (+\infty) = -\infty$, which classical arithmetic leaves undefined; this convention makes the addition total and keeps it associative and commutative.

## Lean subtleties

- It is a monoid, not a group: $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ have no additive inverse, and $\infty - \infty$ cannot be cancelled as with a real number.
- `deriving` means the structure is copied from `WithBot (WithTop ℝ)` rather than written out; the name `instAddCommMonoidEReal` is generated automatically.
- Lean finds this instance by itself wherever a sum of extended reals is written, as with any typeclass instance.

## What it says
For a prime $p$, the $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ form a commutative ring, with the addition and multiplication of the $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$.

- `(p : ℕ)`: a natural number $p$.
- `[hp : Fact (Nat.Prime p)]`: the hypothesis `hp` that $p$ is prime, wrapped in `Fact` so that Lean can find it by itself, as it finds a typeclass instance.
- The conclusion: `CommRing ℤ_[p]`, a commutative ring structure, with a $1$, on `ℤ_[p]`, Mathlib's notation for the $p$-adic integers `PadicInt p`.

The instance has no value of its own: it comes from the `deriving` clause of the definition of `PadicInt`, whose value is `PadicInt.subring p`, the subring of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ made of the $p$-adic numbers of norm at most $1$. The data is that subring's: $0$, $1$, addition, negation and multiplication are those of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, restricted to the closed unit ball, which they preserve since the $p$-adic norm is multiplicative and satisfies the ultrametric inequality.

This is the standard ring $\mathbb{Z}_p = \{x \in \mathbb{Q}_p : |x|_p \le 1\}$, for the same $p$, a prime.

## What it says
The extended real numbers $[-\infty, +\infty]$, with their usual order, form a complete linear order: any two are comparable, and every set of them has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

- The conclusion: `CompleteLinearOrder EReal`, the structure of a complete linear order on `EReal`, Mathlib's extended real line $\mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$.

The instance has no value of its own: it comes from the `deriving` clause of the definition of `EReal`, whose value is `WithBot (WithTop ℝ)`, the reals with a top element $+\infty$ adjoined and then a bottom element $-\infty$. The data is the structure of that type:

- the order: $-\infty$ lies below everything, $+\infty$ above everything, and two reals compare as reals;
- the supremum of a set $S$ is its least upper bound: $-\infty$ when $S$ is empty or $S = \{-\infty\}$, $+\infty$ when $S$ contains $+\infty$ or reals with no real upper bound, and otherwise the real supremum; the infimum is the mirror image;
- the other operations a complete linear order carries, such as binary max and min, which are again fixed by the order.

This is the standard order completion of $\mathbb{R}$ by two endpoints. In a complete lattice the suprema and infima are determined by the order, so once the order is the usual one, nothing else is chosen.

## What it says
If a topological space $\alpha$ is locally connected, then its space of connected components, with the quotient topology, is discrete.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: a topology on $\alpha$, a type (Lean's version of a set) in some universe `u`, which does not affect the mathematics.
- `[LocallyConnectedSpace α]`: $\alpha$ is locally connected: every point has arbitrarily small open connected neighbourhoods, that is, its neighbourhoods have a basis of open connected sets.
- The conclusion: `DiscreteTopology (ConnectedComponents α)`, the space `ConnectedComponents α` is discrete, every subset of it open. That space is the quotient of $\alpha$ that identifies two points when they lie in the same connected component, with the quotient topology: a set of components is open when the union of those components is open in $\alpha$.

As an instance of a class that is a proposition, it provides only this fact, for every locally connected space, and Lean uses it by itself. It is the standard argument: in a locally connected space each connected component is open, so each point of the quotient has an open preimage and is an open point.

## Lean subtleties
- `[TopologicalSpace α]` and `[LocallyConnectedSpace α]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds the topology and the local connectedness by itself; `α` is implicit.
- `ConnectedComponents α` is a quotient type: its elements are the connected components of $\alpha$, and it carries the quotient topology, the finest one making the projection $\alpha \to$ `ConnectedComponents α` continuous.
- The conclusion is about the space of components, not about $\alpha$, which need not be discrete.
- When $\alpha$ is empty, so is its space of components, which is then trivially discrete.
- The hypothesis is sufficient, not necessary: a connected space that is not locally connected, such as the topologist's sine curve, has a single component, so its space of components is a point, which is discrete.

## What it says
The topology Mathlib puts on the natural numbers is the discrete one: every set of natural numbers is open.

- The conclusion: `DiscreteTopology ℕ`, the topology on $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ that Lean finds by itself is the discrete topology, the finest one, in which every subset, and in particular every singleton $\{n\}$, is open.

As an instance of a class that is a proposition, it provides only this fact, and Lean uses it by itself, so that every result about discrete spaces applies to $\mathbb{N}$. The topology itself is a separate instance; this one records that it is discrete. That is the standard topology on $\mathbb{N}$: it is also the topology $\mathbb{N}$ inherits as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$, where each natural number is isolated.

## What it says
The extended nonnegative reals $[0, +\infty]$ carry an extended norm, and the extended norm of each of them is the number itself: $\|x\|_e = x$.

- The conclusion: `ENorm ENNReal`, an extended norm on `ENNReal`, written $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \cup \{\infty\}$ or `ℝ≥0∞` in Mathlib: a function $\|\cdot\|_e$ from it to $[0, +\infty]$.

Its value is `enorm x := x`: the extended norm of $x$ is $x$. So $\|0\|_e = 0$, $\|r\|_e = r$ for a real $r \ge 0$, and $\|\infty\|_e = \infty$.

This is the absolute value of a nonnegative number, which is the number itself, extended to $\infty$ in the only way that keeps it the identity; nothing else would be the natural size of an element of $[0, +\infty]$.

## What it says
The complex numbers form a real inner product space: viewing $\mathbb{C}$ as the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, the inner product is the Euclidean one, $\langle a + bi, c + di\rangle = ac + bd$.

- The conclusion: `InnerProductSpace ℝ ℂ`, a real-valued inner product on $\mathbb{C}$, regarded as a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, that induces the usual absolute value: $\langle z, z\rangle = |z|^2$.

Its value is `InnerProductSpace.complexToReal`, the construction that turns a complex inner product space into a real one by taking the real part of the complex inner product. Applied to $\mathbb{C}$ with its complex inner product $\langle w, z\rangle = \bar w z$, it gives $\langle w, z\rangle_{\mathbb{R}} = \operatorname{Re}(\bar w z)$, which for $w = a + bi$ and $z = c + di$ is $ac + bd$.

This is the standard identification of $\mathbb{C}$ with the Euclidean plane, and its norm is the absolute value $|a + bi| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

## What it says
Every σ-compact topological space is Lindelöf: if $X$ is a countable union of compact subsets, then every open cover of $X$ has a countable subcover.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on $X$, a type (Lean's version of a set) in some universe `u`, which does not affect the mathematics.
- `[SigmaCompactSpace X]`: $X$ is σ-compact, the union of countably many compact subsets.
- The conclusion: `LindelofSpace X`, $X$ is a Lindelöf space: every cover of $X$ by open sets has a countable subfamily that still covers $X$.

As an instance of a class that is a proposition, it provides only this fact, for every σ-compact space, and Lean uses it by itself. The argument is the standard one: given an open cover, each of the countably many compact pieces is covered by finitely many of its sets, and these countably many sets cover $X$. No Hausdorff or local compactness hypothesis is added.

## What it says
If $X$ is locally compact, then $X$ and any topological space $Y$ form a locally compact pair: for every continuous map $f : X \to Y$, every point $x \in X$ and every neighbourhood $s$ of $f(x)$, some compact neighbourhood $K$ of $x$ has $f(K) \subseteq s$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on $X$ and on $Y$, two types (Lean's version of sets).
- `[LocallyCompactSpace X]`: $X$ is locally compact, in the sense that every neighbourhood of every point contains a compact neighbourhood of that point.
- The conclusion: `LocallyCompactPair X Y`, the property of the pair stated above, for every continuous $f : X \to Y$.

As an instance of a class that is a proposition, it provides only this fact, for every locally compact $X$ and every $Y$, and Lean uses it by itself. The reason is short: for continuous $f$, the preimage $f^{-1}(s)$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, and local compactness gives a compact neighbourhood $K$ of $x$ inside it, so $f(K) \subseteq s$. A locally compact pair is Mathlib's weakening of local compactness of $X$, relative to the maps into $Y$; local compactness of $X$ gives it for every $Y$, with no hypothesis on $Y$.

## What it says
A subset of a topological space is connected exactly when it is a connected space in its own right, with the subspace topology.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: a topology on the type $α$ (Lean's version of a set; the implicit `{α : Type u}` only says that $α$ is a type).
- The conclusion: for the implicit subset $s \subseteq α$, `IsConnected s` (the set $s$ is nonempty and cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty pieces open relative to $s$) holds if and only if `ConnectedSpace ↑s` (the space $s$, with the topology it inherits from $α$, is nonempty and is not the union of two disjoint nonempty open subsets).

This is the standard remark that connectedness of a subset is intrinsic: the relatively open subsets of $s$ are exactly the open sets of the subspace $s$, so the two conditions say the same thing. Both include nonemptiness, so the two sides also agree on the empty set.

## What it says
The image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected.

- `[TopologicalSpace α] [TopologicalSpace β]`: topologies on the types $α$ and $β$ (Lean's versions of sets; the implicit `{α : Type u}` and `{β : Type v}` only say that they are types).
- `[ConnectedSpace α]`: the space $α$ is connected: nonempty, and not the union of two disjoint nonempty open subsets.
- `(h : Continuous f)`: the map $f : α \to β$, an implicit argument, is continuous.
- The conclusion: the image `Set.range f` $= \{f(a) : a \in α\} \subseteq β$ is connected (`IsConnected`: nonempty, and not split into two disjoint nonempty pieces open relative to it).

This is the standard theorem that continuous images of connected spaces are connected, stated for the image of the whole space. Nonemptiness passes along too: a point of $α$ gives a point of the image, and a splitting of the image would pull back under $f$ to a splitting of $α$.

## What it says
A map between topological spaces is a homeomorphism exactly when it is continuous and has a continuous two-sided inverse.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on the types $X$ and $Y$ (Lean's versions of sets; the implicit `{X : Type u_1}` and `{Y : Type u_2}` only say that they are types).
- The conclusion: for the implicit map $f : X \to Y$, `IsHomeomorph f` holds if and only if $f$ is continuous and there is a map $g : Y \to X$ with $g(f(x)) = x$ for every $x \in X$ (`Function.LeftInverse g f`), $f(g(y)) = y$ for every $y \in Y$ (`Function.RightInverse g f`), and $g$ continuous.

Mathlib defines `IsHomeomorph f` as: $f$ is continuous, open (it maps open sets to open sets) and bijective. The theorem identifies this with the usual textbook definition of a homeomorphism, a continuous map with a continuous inverse, as the docstring says. No compactness or separation hypothesis enters.

## What it says
In a locally path-connected space, the open path-connected sets containing a point $x$ form a neighbourhood basis at $x$.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: a topology on the type $X$ (Lean's version of a set; the implicit `{X : Type u_1}` only says that $X$ is a type).
- `[LocallyPathConnectedSpace X]`: $X$ is locally path-connected: in Mathlib's formulation, every point has a basis of neighbourhoods that are path-connected, not required to be open.
- `(x : X)`: a point $x$ of $X$.
- The conclusion: `(nhds x).HasBasis (fun s => IsOpen s ∧ x ∈ s ∧ IsPathConnected s) id`, that is, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some open, path-connected set $s$ with $x \in s$.

So every neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ contains an open path-connected neighbourhood of $x$, which is the usual textbook definition of local path-connectedness; the theorem shows that Mathlib's weaker-looking class, whose basic neighbourhoods need not be open, gives this open form.

## What it says
A subset of a product of two topological spaces is open exactly when each of its points lies in an open rectangle inside it.

## What it says
A subset of the disjoint union of two topological spaces is open exactly when its parts in the two pieces are open in them.

- `[TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]`: topologies on the types $X$ and $Y$ (Lean's versions of sets; the implicit `{X : Type u}` and `{Y : Type v}` only say that they are types). The disjoint union `X ⊕ Y` then carries the disjoint-union topology.

This is the usual definition of the topology of a disjoint union (the coproduct of spaces): the finest topology for which both inclusions are continuous, whose open sets are exactly those described. Mathlib builds that topology from the two inclusions, and this theorem unfolds it into the textbook description. No hypothesis is placed on $X$, $Y$ or $s$.

## What it says
A union of preconnected sets that all share a common point is preconnected.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: a topology on the type $α$ (Lean's version of a set; the implicit `{α : Type u}` only says that $α$ is a type). The family is indexed by the implicit `ι`, which may be any index type, and consists of the implicit sets $s_i \subseteq α$.

This is the standard theorem that the union of a family of connected sets with a point in common is connected, stated with preconnectedness: if a splitting of the union existed, the common point would lie in one piece, and each $s_i$, being preconnected and containing that point, would lie entirely in that piece, leaving the other empty.

## What it says
A subset $s$ of a topological space $\alpha$ is preconnected exactly when every cover of $s$ by two closed sets that do not meet inside $s$ puts $s$ inside one of them.

- `[TopologicalSpace α]`: $\alpha$ carries a topology. Here $\alpha$ is any type and $s$ any subset of it, both left implicit.
- The conclusion: `IsPreconnected s` holds if and only if, for all subsets $u, v$ of $\alpha$ that are closed (`IsClosed u`, `IsClosed v`), with $s \subseteq u \cup v$ and $s \cap (u \cap v) = \emptyset$, either $s \subseteq u$ or $s \subseteq v$.

`IsPreconnected s` is Mathlib's notion of a connected subspace without the demand that it be nonempty: $s$ cannot be split by two open sets of $\alpha$ that both meet $s$ and do not meet each other inside $s$. This theorem phrases the same notion with closed sets. The sets $s \cap u$ and $s \cap v$ are closed in the subspace $s$, cover it and are disjoint, so the standard criterion (the subspace is not the disjoint union of two nonempty relatively closed parts) says that one of them is empty, that is, $s$ lies in the other. Every relatively closed subset of $s$ has the form $s \cap u$ with $u$ closed in $\alpha$, so the criterion is the classical one for the subspace topology.

- `(H : ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, ∃ t ⊆ s, x ∈ t ∧ y ∈ t ∧ IsPreconnected t)`: for all points $x, y$ of $s$ there is a subset $t$ of $s$ that contains both and is preconnected.
- The conclusion: `IsPreconnected s`, that is, $s$ cannot be split by two open sets of $\alpha$ that both meet $s$ and do not meet each other inside $s$.

This is the standard principle behind the proof that path-connected sets are connected: it is enough to join any two points by a connected piece of the set, a path's image being one such piece. The hypothesis is also necessary, since a preconnected $s$ can take $t = s$ for every pair, so the statement loses nothing.

## What it says
A map $f : E \to X$ is the quotient map of $E$ by a covering space action of a group $G$ exactly when $f$ is a surjective covering map, $G$ acts on $E$ freely and by homeomorphisms, and the fibres of $f$ are the $G$-orbits.

- `[TopologicalSpace E] [TopologicalSpace X]`: $E$ and $X$ are topological spaces, any types each with a topology.
- `(f : E → X)`: a map $f$ from $E$ to $X$; no continuity is assumed here, since both sides imply it.
- `[Group G] [MulAction G E]`: $G$ is a group, given as a type `(G : Type u_3)`, acting on $E$ on the left, written $g \cdot e$; it carries no topology.
- The conclusion: `IsQuotientCoveringMap f G` holds if and only if all of the following hold:
  - `IsCoveringMap f`: every point of $X$ has an open neighbourhood whose preimage is a disjoint union of open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto it;
  - `Function.Surjective f`: $f$ is onto;
  - `ContinuousConstSMul G E`: each translation $e \mapsto g \cdot e$ is continuous, hence a homeomorphism, with inverse the translation by $g^{-1}$;
  - `IsCancelSMul G E`: $g \cdot e = h \cdot e$ forces $g = h$, so the action is free (the other cancellation, $g \cdot e = g \cdot e'$ forcing $e = e'$, holds in any group action);
  - for all $e_1, e_2 \in E$, $f(e_1) = f(e_2)$ if and only if $e_1$ lies in the orbit `MulAction.orbit G e₂` $= \{g \cdot e_2 : g \in G\}$.

`IsQuotientCoveringMap f G` is the classical situation of a covering space action: $f$ is a quotient map whose fibres are the orbits, and each point of $E$ has a neighbourhood disjoint from its translates by every $g \neq 1$. Such a quotient map is a covering; conversely, for a covering whose fibres are the orbits of a free action, a sheet over an evenly covered set meets none of its nontrivial translates, since $f$ is injective on it.

## What it says
If a group $G$ acts freely, by homeomorphisms and properly discontinuously on a locally compact Hausdorff space $E$, then the projection of $E$ onto its orbit space $E/G$ is the quotient map of a covering space action of $G$.

- `[TopologicalSpace E]`: $E$ is a topological space, any type with a topology.
- `[Group G] [MulAction G E]`: $G$ is a group acting on $E$ on the left, written $g \cdot e$; $G$ carries no topology.
- `[ContinuousConstSMul G E]`: each translation $e \mapsto g \cdot e$ is continuous, hence a homeomorphism of $E$.
- `[ProperlyDiscontinuousSMul G E]`: for any two compact sets $K, L \subseteq E$, only finitely many $g \in G$ have $g \cdot K$ meeting $L$.
- `[LocallyCompactSpace E] [T2Space E]`: $E$ is locally compact (every neighbourhood of a point contains a compact one) and Hausdorff.
- `[IsCancelSMul G E]`: $g \cdot e = h \cdot e$ forces $g = h$: the action is free.
- The conclusion: `IsQuotientCoveringMap (Quotient.mk (MulAction.orbitRel G E)) G`. Here `MulAction.orbitRel G E` is the equivalence relation "lies in the same $G$-orbit", and `Quotient.mk` sends $e$ to its orbit $Ge$ in the orbit space $E/G$, with the quotient topology. The conclusion says this projection is a quotient map whose fibres are the orbits, and that each point of $E$ has a neighbourhood disjoint from all its translates by $g \neq 1$, which makes the projection a covering map.

This is the standard theorem that a free, properly discontinuous action on a Hausdorff space is a covering space action, so that $E \to E/G$ is a covering. Local compactness is assumed because properly discontinuous is taken here in its compact-set form: a compact neighbourhood of a point then meets only finitely many of its translates, and the Hausdorff property and freeness shrink it to one that meets none.

## What it says
A subset $s$ of a topological space $X$ is σ-compact, a countable union of compact subsets of $X$, exactly when $s$ with its subspace topology is a σ-compact space.

- `[TopologicalSpace X]`: $X$ carries a topology. Here $X$ is any type and $s$ any subset of it, both left implicit.
- The conclusion: `IsSigmaCompact s`, there are compact subsets $K_0, K_1, K_2, \dots$ of $X$ whose union is $s$, holds if and only if `SigmaCompactSpace ↑s`, the space $s$, with the topology it inherits from $X$, is the union of countably many of its own compact subsets.

The two sides say the same thing because compactness of a subset $K \subseteq s$ does not depend on whether it is taken in $s$ or in $X$: an open cover of $K$ in one gives one in the other, by intersecting with $s$ or by extending open sets of $s$ to open sets of $X$. So a sequence of compact pieces covering $s$ serves on both sides. This is the standard fact that σ-compactness of a subset is intrinsic to it. No hypothesis on $s$ is needed: it need not be closed, and $X$ need not be Hausdorff.
